6.title: Cranial Nerve I (The Olfactory Nerve)
6.subtitle: Where a smell deficit places the lesion: nasal disease, nerve filaments, bulb/tract, or frontal-temporal cortex

points.text: Olfactory filaments cross the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to reach the olfactory bulb, so a cribriform fracture can tear them.
points.quote: These bundles, the filaments of the olfactory nerve, penetrate the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone and enter the olfactory bulb.

points.text: In the bulb the afferent fibers synapse on the second-order neurons, the mitral and tufted cells.
points.quote: the olfactory afferent fibers synapse with the dendrites of the second-order neurons called the mitral and tufted cells

points.text: The tract runs back in the olfactory sulcus on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, which is why frontal masses can reach it.
points.quote: The axons of the mitral and tufted cells leave the olfactory bulb and course posteriorly, as the olfactory tract, in the olfactory sulcus

points.text: Some strial fibers cross in the anterior commissure to the opposite hemisphere; others go to the ipsilateral piriform lobe.
points.quote: Some of these strial fibers decussate in the anterior commissure and join the fibers from the opposite olfactory pathways

points.text: The piriform cortex is the largest cortical olfactory area, at the frontal-temporal junction.
points.quote: The piriform cortex (area 51) is the largest cortical olfactory area

points.text: Test each nostril separately with nonirritating substances; perceiving a smell matters more than naming it.
points.quote: perception of the smell is of more value than identification of the specific substance

points.text: Avoid ammonia-type irritants, because they stimulate trigeminal fibers rather than purely testing CN I.
points.quote: Irritating substances (e.g., ammonia) are to be avoided because they stimulate the trigeminal nerve fibers in the nasal mucosa

localizationRules.explanation: Before localizing to the nervous system, look for local nasal disease or an upper respiratory infection, especially when the loss is bilateral.
localizationRules.quote: must first be sought as the cause of anosmia, especially if the olfactory difficulty is bilateral

localizationRules.rule: Unilateral anosmia points to the pre-decussation pathway
localizationRules.explanation: After nasal disease is excluded, unilateral anosmia suggests a lesion of the filaments, bulb, tract or stria.
localizationRules.quote: anosmia, especially unilateral anosmia, should raise the suspicion of a lesion affecting the olfactory nerve filaments, bulb, tract, or stria

localizationRules.rule: Distal to the decussation, no deficit
localizationRules.explanation: Cortical representation is bilateral, so a unilateral lesion beyond the crossing does not cause anosmia.
localizationRules.quote: a unilateral lesion distal to the decussation of the olfactory fibers causes no olfactory impairment

localizationRules.explanation: Frontal lobe masses may produce anosmia before obvious frontal signs, so test smell in any patient with personality change or subtle frontal signs.
localizationRules.quote: often exert pressure on the olfactory system and may lead to anosmia even before clear-cut frontal lobe signs

localizationRules.rule: Trauma disrupts fibers before the decussation
localizationRules.explanation: Head injury is a leading cause of anosmia through damage to the olfactory fibers, with or without a fracture.
localizationRules.quote: is probably the most common cause of disruption of the olfactory fibers before their decussation

keySyndromes.name: Foster-Kennedy syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral anosmia + ipsilateral optic atrophy + contralateral papilledema
keySyndromes.clue: Seen with olfactory groove or sphenoid ridge masses or frontal space-occupying lesions; the atrophy is on the side of the mass and the papilledema on the opposite side.
keySyndromes.quote: The Foster-Kennedy syndrome is occasionally noted with olfactory groove or sphenoid ridge masses (especially meningiomas) or space-occupying lesions of the frontal lobe.

keySyndromes.name: Pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Previous unilateral optic atrophy + raised intracranial pressure of any cause + papilledema only in the other eye
keySyndromes.clue: Unlike the true syndrome, no frontal mass is required; the atrophic disc cannot swell.
keySyndromes.quote: Because the atrophic disc cannot become swollen, only the previously normal fundus demonstrates papilledema.

keySyndromes.name: Esthesioneuroblastoma
keySyndromes.triad: Anosmia + persistent nasal obstruction + epistaxis
keySyndromes.clue: Arises from olfactory neuroepithelium near the ethmoid sinus and may extend into the orbit.
keySyndromes.quote: These tumors may present with anosmia as well as persistent nasal obstruction and epistaxis

keySyndromes.name: Kallmann syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Permanent anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (+ possible cerebellar ataxia and mirror movements)
keySyndromes.clue: A familial syndrome combining a smell deficit with an endocrine deficit.
keySyndromes.quote: A familial syndrome of permanent anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome) has also been described

keySyndromes.name: Olfactory epileptic aura
keySyndromes.triad: Olfactory hallucination + partial seizure with complex symptomatology (+ amygdala as likely symptomatogenic zone)
keySyndromes.clue: The aura is not necessarily unpleasant; tumors are the commonest cause in this group.
keySyndromes.quote: In patients with olfactory epileptic auras, tumors are the most common etiology of the seizures, and mesial temporal sclerosis is relatively rare

boardTraps.text: The side of impact matters: frontal blows cause less olfactory dysfunction than occipital or lateral blows.
boardTraps.quote: Frontal impact produces less dysfunction than back (occipital) or side impacts

boardTraps.text: Anosmia does not require a fracture; closed head injury alone can disrupt the pathways on one or both sides.
boardTraps.quote: but closed head injury without fracture may also disrupt the olfactory pathways unilaterally or bilaterally

boardTraps.text: Many cases labelled Foster-Kennedy may in fact be due to compression of both optic nerves.
boardTraps.quote: Many cases of Foster-Kennedy syndrome may actually be due to direct bilateral optic nerve compression

boardTraps.text: A pseudo-Foster-Kennedy picture is most often sequential anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or optic neuritis.
boardTraps.quote: A pseudo-Foster-Kennedy syndrome is most often due to sequential anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (arteritic or nonarteritic) or optic neuritis

boardTraps.text: Anosmia is expected in Parkinson disease; anosmia in suspected PSP or corticobasal degeneration is atypical and should prompt diagnostic review.
boardTraps.quote: Anosmia in suspected progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration is atypical and should likewise provoke diagnostic review.

boardTraps.text: Olfactory damage after anterior communicating aneurysm surgery depends on the approach.
boardTraps.quote: Olfactory damage is much more common after an anterior interhemispheric surgical approach rather than after a basal interhemispheric approach.

7.title: Visual Pathways
7.subtitle: Reading a visual field defect, acuity change and pupil sign to place the lesion from retina to occipital cortex

points.text: Temporal-retina axons stay ipsilateral to the lateral geniculate body, while nasal-retina axons cross at the chiasm.
points.quote: The axons of the ganglion cells on the temporal side of a vertical line drawn through the fovea project to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate body

points.text: At the chiasm slightly more than half of the fibers cross (53:47), and these come from the nasal retina.
points.quote: more than half of the fibers (those originating in ganglion cells of the nasal retina) cross to reach the contralateral optic tract

points.text: The crossed:uncrossed ratio in the chiasm is a number worth remembering for chiasmal field analysis.
points.quote: The ratio of crossed and uncrossed fibers in the chiasm is 53:47.

points.text: Retinal nerve fibers respect the horizontal meridian only in the nasal visual field, because the raphe lies in the temporal retina.
points.quote: the nerve fiber layer of the retina respects the horizontal meridian only in the nasal field, not in the temporal field

points.text: The LGN is a thalamic relay for all retinal ganglion cell axons that subserve vision.
points.quote: The lateral geniculate body, a thalamic nucleus, provides a relay station for all the axons of the retinal ganglion cells subserving vision.

points.text: LGN laminae alternate between the two eyes: I, IV and VI are contralateral, II, III and V ipsilateral.
points.quote: Layers I, IV, and VI serve the contralateral eye, whereas II, III, and V are connected with the ipsilateral eye.

points.text: Upper-field fibers go through the parietal lobe.
points.quote: Upper field fibers originate in the medial aspect of lateral geniculate nucleus and travel through the parietal lobes

points.text: Lower-field fibers loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop).
points.quote: lower field fibers originate from the lateral aspect of the lateral geniculate body and make a loop in the temporal lobe

points.text: Primary visual cortex (area 17) lies along the calcarine fissure on the medial occipital surface.
points.quote: Cortical area 17 of Brodmann, located along the superior and inferior lips of the calcarine fissure in the medial aspect of the occipital lobe

points.text: Each occipital lobe sees the opposite visual hemifield, because it receives the same-side half of each retina.
points.quote: More simply, it receives projections from the two halves of the retinas on the same side as the occipital lobe

points.text: Macula is represented posteriorly, periphery anteriorly in the calcarine cortex.
points.quote: the macular retina is represented in the posterior pole of the calcarine cortex, whereas the more peripheral retina is more anteriorly represented

points.text: Complete central retinal artery occlusion gives global retinal ischemia unless a cilioretinal artery supplies the macula.
points.quote: the complete occlusion of the central retinal artery results in global retinal ischemia, except when the macular area is supplied by cilioretinal arteries

points.text: The optic tract also receives the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid.
points.quote: which, in addition, is fed by the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid

points.text: The LGN has a dual supply: anterior choroidal laterally, lateral posterior choroidal medially.
points.quote: The lateral geniculate body receives a dual supply, from the anterior choroidal artery laterally and the lateral posterior choroidal artery medially.

points.text: The upper radiations are supplied by the middle cerebral artery, the lower by the posterior cerebral artery.
points.quote: The upper (parietal) portion of the optic radiations is supplied by branches of the middle cerebral artery

points.text: The calcarine branch of the PCA supplies the primary visual cortex.
points.quote: The posterior cerebral artery, particularly its calcarine branch running in the calcarine fissure, supplies the primary visual cortex.

localizationRules.explanation: A monocular field defect points to the retina or optic nerve; a binocular defect places the lesion at or beyond the chiasm.
localizationRules.quote: whether the field defect is monocular, in which case the lesion usually affects the retina or the optic nerve, or binocular

localizationRules.explanation: Most optic neuropathies reduce acuity, so a visual field defect with preserved acuity should make you think of preretinal, retinal or retrochiasmal disease.
localizationRules.quote: Also, most optic neuropathies involve VA; spared acuity should raise the suspicion of preretinal, retinal, or retrochiasmal disease

localizationRules.explanation: Tract and LGN hemianopias tend to be incongruous; the further back the lesion, the more the two eyes' defects match.
localizationRules.quote: the more posteriorly the lesion is located in the optic pathways, the greater the congruity of the defect in either field

localizationRules.explanation: A tract lesion can cause a modest RAPD in the eye contralateral to the lesion (the eye with temporal field loss).
localizationRules.quote: Optic tract disease may cause a modest RAPD when the light is directed into the eye contralateral to the lesion

localizationRules.explanation: Lesions of the LGN and geniculocalcarine pathway leave the light reflex intact, because pupillary afferents leave before the LGN.
localizationRules.quote: Lateral geniculate body lesions and those in the geniculocalcarine segment of the optic sensory pathways leave the pupillary light reflex unimpaired.

keySyndromes.name: Body of the chiasm syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Bitemporal field defects (peripheral and/or central, with or without macular splitting) + usually normal visual acuity + normal or pale optic discs
keySyndromes.clue: Bitemporal defects are most often due to a compressive mass such as a pituitary tumor.
keySyndromes.quote: Body of the chiasm syndrome, in which patients demonstrate bitemporal visual field defects

keySyndromes.name: Anterior chiasm (junctional) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Central defect in one eye + superior temporal defect in the other eye
keySyndromes.clue: Reflects damage to the ipsilateral optic nerve at its junction with the chiasm; test the field of the apparently normal eye.
keySyndromes.quote: central defect in one field with a superior temporal defect in the opposite field points to the involvement of the anterior angle of the chiasm

keySyndromes.name: Optic tract lesion
keySyndromes.triad: Incongruous homonymous hemianopia (macula-splitting if complete) + RAPD in the contralateral eye + normal visual acuity
keySyndromes.clue: Chronic lesions may produce hemianopic optic atrophy (bow-tie pallor in the contralateral eye).
keySyndromes.quote: afferent pupillary defect in the contralateral eye in a patient with normal VA bilaterally and a complete HH are usually indicative of optic tract involvement

keySyndromes.name: Lateral geniculate body: anterior choroidal artery
keySyndromes.triad: Congruous homonymous defect in upper and lower quadrants + sparing of a horizontal sector (quadruple sectoranopia) + sectorial optic atrophy
keySyndromes.clue: Posterior choroidal artery interruption instead causes a horizontal wedge-shaped sector defect.
keySyndromes.quote: Occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery may cause a homonymous defect in the upper and lower quadrants with the sparing of a horizontal sector

keySyndromes.name: Parietal optic radiations
keySyndromes.triad: Inferior quadrantic defect (pie on the floor) + more congruous than temporal lesions + other parietal signs
keySyndromes.clue: Large lesions can give complete macula-splitting hemianopia; parietal lesions more often betray themselves by other neurologic signs.
keySyndromes.quote: The involvement of the optic radiations in the depth of the parietal lobe gives rise to an inferior quadrantic defect

keySyndromes.name: Medial occipital lesion
keySyndromes.triad: Highly congruous homonymous hemianopia + macular sparing when both calcarine banks are involved + posterior cerebral artery infarct as the common cause
keySyndromes.clue: Complete HH with macular sparing points to the occipital cortex.
keySyndromes.quote: When both the upper and lower calcarine cortices are affected, a complete HH, usually with macular sparing, develops

boardTraps.text: Wilbrand knee may be an artifact of enucleation, yet junctional field loss still localizes to the junction of optic nerve and chiasm.
boardTraps.quote: whether Wilbrand knee exists anatomically, the localizing value of junctional visual field loss to the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm remains undiminished

boardTraps.text: A complete homonymous hemianopia does not localize within the retrochiasmal pathway.
boardTraps.quote: Complete HHs are nonlocalizing and may be seen with any lesion of the retrochiasmal pathway

boardTraps.text: Congruity helps but is not a strict rule: many tract and radiation lesions give congruent defects, especially after stroke.
boardTraps.quote: although lesions involving the occipital lobe characteristically produce congruent HH, at least 50% of lesions in other locations also produce congruent HH

boardTraps.text: The monocular temporal crescent is the one retrochiasmal field defect that can be strictly unilateral.
boardTraps.quote: This is the only retrochiasmatic lesion that may cause a strictly unilateral visual field defect

boardTraps.text: Bitemporal defects that cross the vertical midline are pseudochiasmal and may reflect ametropia, tilted discs or other eye disease.
boardTraps.quote: Pseudochiasmal visual field defects (i.e., bitemporal defects that do not respect the vertical midline) may also be due to ametropia

boardTraps.text: Pure occipital lesions leave the patient aware of the hemianopia; larger or more anterior lesions may not.
boardTraps.quote: Patients with purely occipital lesions are partially or fully aware of the hemianopia, whereas patients with larger or more anterior lesions

9.title: Cranial Nerve V (The Trigeminal Nerve)
9.subtitle: Sorting facial numbness, pain and jaw weakness into supranuclear, nuclear, root, ganglion and peripheral-branch lesions

points.text: Supranuclear control comes from the lower precentral gyrus.
points.quote: It receives its supranuclear control through corticobulbar fibers originating in the lower third of the precentral gyrus.

points.text: The bilateral corticobulbar connections descend through the corona radiata, internal capsule and peduncle and cross in the pons before reaching the motor nuclei.
points.quote: These bilateral connections travel through the corona radiata, internal capsule, and cerebral peduncle and decussate in the pons before supplying the motor nuclei.

points.text: The motor root leaves the skull with V3 through the foramen ovale and joins it to form the mandibular nerve, which supplies the masticatory muscles.
points.quote: After leaving the skull, the motor root joins the mandibular (third) division of the trigeminal nerve to form the mandibular nerve

points.text: The spinal nucleus carries pain, temperature and soft touch from the face and mucous membranes.
points.quote: receives fibers that convey the sensations of pain, temperature, and soft touch from the face and mucous membranes

points.text: The main sensory nucleus, in the lateral pons, serves tactile and proprioceptive sensation.
points.quote: Fibers entering this nucleus are concerned with tactile and proprioceptive sensation.

points.text: The mesencephalic nucleus receives proprioception from the masticatory muscles and from muscles of other motor cranial nerves.
points.quote: This nucleus receives proprioceptive impulses from the masticatory muscles and from muscles supplied by other motor cranial nerves.

points.text: Ophthalmic fibers lie ventral in the spinal tract and reach the lowest levels; mandibular fibers lie dorsal and end most rostrally.
points.quote: The fibers of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve travel in the most ventral part of the spinal tract

points.text: The rostral-caudal arrangement of the spinal nucleus (perioral rostral, lateral face caudal) underlies the onionskin pattern.
points.quote: This onionskin segmental distribution reflects the rostral-caudal somatotopy of the cutaneous distribution of the spinal nucleus

points.text: V1 runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus beside CN III, IV and VI and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
points.quote: lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus in close association with the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves

points.text: V2 passes through the inferolateral cavernous sinus and exits via the foramen rotundum.
points.quote: through the inferolateral portion of the cavernous sinus and then leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum

points.text: V3 exits through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa.
points.quote: This nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale and travels in the infratemporal fossa

points.text: The lingual branch carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; taste travels with the facial nerve.
points.quote: the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (not taste sensation, which is carried by the facial nerve)

localizationRules.explanation: A lesion distal to the gasserian ganglion affects one division's skin territory; a lesion at or proximal to the ganglion affects the whole ipsilateral face.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of individual divisions (distal to the gasserian ganglion) result in sensory loss confined to the cutaneous supply of that division

localizationRules.explanation: Pain/temperature loss with preserved touch points to the spinal tract and nucleus rather than the main sensory nucleus.
localizationRules.quote: differentiates lesions affecting the spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve from lesions affecting the main sensory nucleus

localizationRules.rule: Jaw deviation with nuclear or infranuclear lesions
localizationRules.explanation: With a motor nucleus or peripheral motor lesion the jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening, because the opposite lateral pterygoid acts unopposed.
localizationRules.quote: the jaw deviates to the paralyzed side when the mouth is opened (due to contraction of the contralateral intact lateral pterygoid muscle)

localizationRules.explanation: Cortical control is bilateral with a contralateral predominance for the masseter, so unilateral lesions give mild weakness; bilateral upper motor neuron lesions give marked weakness.
localizationRules.quote: Supranuclear control of trigeminal motor function is bilateral; however, the contralateral hemisphere exerts predominant control on the voluntary activity of the masseter

localizationRules.explanation: The afferent limb is V1 and the efferent limb is the facial nerve on both sides, so a trigeminal lesion abolishes both the direct and the consensual response.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of the trigeminal nerve result in loss of the ipsilateral and contralateral responses.

keySyndromes.name: Wallenberg syndrome (trigeminal component)
keySyndromes.triad: Loss of pain and temperature over the ipsilateral face + often contralateral body and limb sensory loss + spinal trigeminal nucleus involvement
keySyndromes.clue: The spinal nucleus is characteristically affected; the typical pattern is loss over the whole side of the face.
keySyndromes.quote: In the typical syndrome, pain and temperature sensation are lost over the entire side of the face.

keySyndromes.name: Cerebellopontine angle extension
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral facial pain, paresthesias and sensory loss + masticatory paresis + depressed corneal reflex + ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness and vertigo
keySyndromes.clue: Usually vestibular schwannoma or meningioma; cranial nerve VIII involvement distinguishes it from a pure trigeminal lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: Ipsilateral facial pain, paresthesias, sensory loss, masticatory paresis, and a depressed corneal reflex are then associated with ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness, and vertigo

keySyndromes.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
keySyndromes.triad: Sudden lancinating unilateral pain in one or more divisions + brief paroxysms + triggers from non-nociceptive facial stimulation
keySyndromes.clue: V2 is the most frequent territory, then V3 and V1; many cases are due to vascular compression or irritation of the root entry zone.
keySyndromes.quote: The painful paroxysms are often triggered by non-nociceptive facial stimulation and are often associated with facial contortions.

keySyndromes.name: Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral miosis and ptosis without facial anhidrosis + ipsilateral trigeminal involvement (+ possible CN IV and VI involvement)
keySyndromes.clue: Usually a middle cranial fossa lesion between the trigeminal ganglion and the internal carotid artery near the petrous apex.
keySyndromes.quote: This uncommon syndrome is composed of two essential components: unilateral oculosympathetic paresis and evidence of trigeminal involvement on the same side

keySyndromes.name: Gradenigo syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral pain and sensory disturbance in V1 + ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (+ oculosympathetic paresis without anhidrosis)
keySyndromes.clue: A lesion at the petrous apex affects V1 and the abducens nerve.
keySyndromes.quote: Pain and sensory disturbance in the upper part of the face (ophthalmic distribution) are then associated with ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy

keySyndromes.name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ophthalmoplegia + pain, paresthesias and sensory loss in V1 (less often V2) + occasional oculosympathetic paresis
keySyndromes.clue: V3 is spared, so there is no masticatory weakness.
keySyndromes.quote: Because the mandibular nerve is spared, no masticatory paresis is evident.

boardTraps.text: The angle of the jaw is supplied by cervical roots (C2-C3), not by V; hemifacial loss that spares it favors an organic lesion.
boardTraps.quote: and not by the trigeminal nerve. Therefore, a hemifacial sensory loss that spares the angle of the jaw is probably organic

boardTraps.text: In Wallenberg syndrome the textbook dissociated trigeminal pattern was actually uncommon in one series of 50 patients; onionskin patterns were more often seen than divisional ones.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, in this study, the so-called classic dissociated sensory pattern of lateral medullary infarction was actually uncommon

boardTraps.text: Superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus lesions look alike clinically and usually need neuroimaging to separate them.
boardTraps.quote: the superior orbital fissure syndrome and the cavernous sinus syndrome usually cannot be differentiated clinically without the use of neuroradiologic procedures

boardTraps.text: A numb chin (mental neuropathy) without trauma should trigger a search for malignancy.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, patients who develop a nontraumatic mental neuropathy should undergo a careful search for malignancy

boardTraps.text: Jaw-closing weakness points to myasthenia gravis, jaw-opening weakness to muscle disease, in flaccid quadriparesis.
boardTraps.quote: the presence of jaw-closing weakness pointed toward myasthenia gravis, whereas the presence of jaw-opening weakness suggested muscle disease

boardTraps.text: A mesencephalic nucleus lesion is nearly silent, at most depressing the ipsilateral jaw jerk.
boardTraps.quote: cause no apparent neurologic signs and symptoms, except perhaps depression of the ipsilateral jaw jerk

10.title: Cranial Nerve VII (The Facial Nerve)
10.subtitle: Tell central from peripheral facial palsy, then place a peripheral lesion by taste, hearing and tearing

points.text: The facial motor nucleus sits in the caudal pontine tegmentum, dorsal to the superior olive.
points.quote: Fibers of the motor division arise from the facial motor nucleus, located in the ventrolateral caudal pontine tegmentum, dorsal to the superior olive

points.text: The intrapontine fascicle loops around the abducens nucleus as the genu, which is why pontine lesions can involve both CN VI and CN VII.
points.quote: These roots then sweep from medial to lateral around the dorsal surface of the abducens nucleus as the genu of the facial nerve

points.text: Voluntary facial movement is driven by corticobulbar fibers from the lower precentral gyrus.
points.quote: Supranuclear control of facial movements is mediated through corticobulbar fibers originating from the lower third of the precentral gyrus.

points.text: The part of the nucleus supplying the upper face has bilateral supranuclear control, so a supranuclear lesion spares the forehead.
points.quote: supplying the upper muscles of facial expression such as the frontalis and orbicularis oculi, is spared due to its bilateral supranuclear control

points.text: Emotional (involuntary) facial movement uses a separate pathway that does not run in the internal capsule.
points.quote: Fibers mediating emotional facial movements do not descend within the internal capsule in their course to the facial motor nuclei.

points.text: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the nervus intermedius, a thinner nerve than the motor root.
points.quote: Taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by a thinner nerve, the nervus intermedius of Wrisberg

points.text: The greater superficial petrosal nerve arises at the geniculate ganglion and carries parasympathetic fibers for tearing.
points.quote: arising from the apex of the geniculate ganglion, is composed of preganglionic parasympathetic efferents innervating the lacrimal, palatal, and nasal glands

points.text: In the mastoid segment the stapedius nerve branches off first, then the chorda tympani, which joins the lingual nerve.
points.quote: the nerve to the stapedius muscle originates near the upper end, and the other branch, the chorda tympani, joins the lingual nerve

points.text: The chorda tympani also carries taste afferents toward the nucleus tractus solitarius.
points.quote: The chorda tympani also contains afferent taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue destined for the nucleus tractus solitarius.

points.text: The intracranial segment of the nerve is supplied by AICA.
points.quote: The intracranial segment of the facial nerve receives its blood supply from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)

coreAnatomy.title: Bedside tests that place the lesion

points.text: Taste, hyperacusis and tearing each point to a different branch, so together they locate the lesion along the nerve.
points.quote: The lesion site can be deduced by assessing whether there is preservation or impairment of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani),

points.text: Stapedius involvement makes low tones sound louder on the affected side.
points.quote: Hyperacusis resulting from stapedius muscle involvement is more notable for low tones that sound louder on the affected side.

points.text: The facial nerve is the efferent limb of the corneal and palpebral reflexes, which are depressed on the side of a lower motor neuron lesion.
points.quote: The facial nerve is the efferent limb of the corneal and palpebral reflexes, which are ipsilaterally depressed with lower motor neuron

localizationRules.explanation: Contralateral weakness of voluntary facial movement with relative sparing of forehead and orbicularis oculi; the mouth region is most affected.
localizationRules.quote: there is paresis of voluntary movements of the muscles of facial expression contralateral to the affected hemisphere, with relative sparing of the frontalis and orbicularis oculi

localizationRules.rule: Nuclear or fascicular lesion = peripheral palsy
localizationRules.explanation: A complete pontine lesion of the nucleus or fascicle gives an ipsilateral palsy of the whole face, including the forehead, so look for neighbouring pontine signs.
localizationRules.quote: With complete lesions, there is unilateral ipsilateral paralysis of all mimetic facial muscles, with loss of frontal wrinkling

localizationRules.explanation: CN VII is next to the nervus intermedius and CN VIII there, so expect facial weakness with impaired taste plus ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness and vertigo, and look for pons, cerebellar and trigeminal signs.
localizationRules.quote: Cerebellopontine angle lesions frequently involve neighboring structures, including the pons (nystagmus or ipsilateral gaze palsy), cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum (ipsilateral ataxia)

localizationRules.rule: Lesion in the facial canal: tearing
localizationRules.explanation: Whether tearing is impaired tells you if the lesion is proximal or distal to the greater superficial petrosal nerve.
localizationRules.quote: With lesions proximal to the greater superficial petrosal nerve, lacrimation is impaired; with distal lesions, lacrimation is normal.

localizationRules.rule: Lesion after the stapedius and chorda tympani
localizationRules.explanation: Between the stapedius branch and the chorda tympani, taste is lost but hearing is spared; distal to the chorda tympani only the motor palsy remains.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions in this segment result in peripheral facial paralysis without hyperacusis or impaired taste.

keySyndromes.name: Millard-Gubler syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Ipsilateral lateral rectus paralysis + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Ventral pontine lesion that includes the corticospinal tract; compare with Foville, where the gaze center is involved instead of the lateral rectus.
keySyndromes.quote: results from ventral pontine lesions interrupting the fascicles of the facial and abducens nerves and the corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Foville syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Paralysis of conjugate gaze to the side of the lesion + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Pontine tegmental lesion involving the PPRF, so the gaze palsy is conjugate toward the lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: The Foville syndrome results from pontine tegmental lesions interrupting the fascicles of the facial nerve, the PPRF, and the corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Eight-and-a-half syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) plus horizontal gaze palsy + Ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy
keySyndromes.clue: One-and-a-half syndrome plus ipsilateral facial palsy from a dorsal caudal pontine tegmental lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: The eight-and-a-half syndrome results from dorsal tegmental caudal pontine lesions involving the PPRF or the abducens nucleus, the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)

keySyndromes.name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion)
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Hyperacusis + Impaired taste + Geniculate neuralgia + Herpetic vesicles of eardrum, external auditory meatus or palate
keySyndromes.clue: Reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion; the book notes that some cases occur without a rash (zoster sine herpete).
keySyndromes.quote: hyperacusis, impaired taste, geniculate neuralgia, and herpetic vesicles involving the eardrum, external auditory meatus, or palate

keySyndromes.name: Bell palsy
keySyndromes.triad: Acute onset + Unilateral lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial muscles + Often preceded by ear pain, dysgeusia, hyperacusis or decreased tearing
keySyndromes.clue: Idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion; the book gives red flags (for example gradual progression beyond 3 weeks) that point elsewhere.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a common (up to 40/100,000) acute monosymptomatic, idiopathic, unilateral, lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial muscles

keySyndromes.name: Hemifacial spasm
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral intermittent involuntary spasms + Usually start in orbicularis oculi and spread to other ipsilateral facial muscles + Often a vascular loop at the root exit zone
keySyndromes.clue: A hyperactive, not weak, facial nerve; compression at the root exit zone in the cerebellopontine angle is the most common cause.
keySyndromes.quote: unilateral, intermittent, involuntary, hyperactive dysfunction of the seventh CN, most commonly due to a vascular loop abutting the facial nerve at the root exit zone

boardTraps.text: Voluntary and emotional facial movements can dissociate: voluntary paresis without emotional paresis is the far more common pattern after corticobulbar interruption.
boardTraps.quote: Volitional facial paresis without emotional is far more common than emotional facial paresis and results from interruption of corticobulbar pathways

boardTraps.text: The Bell phenomenon (eye rolling up and out on attempted closure) is a normal response that only becomes visible when the eyelid cannot close.
boardTraps.quote: The Bell phenomenon represents a normal response that becomes apparent due to paralysis of eyelid closure.

boardTraps.text: Not every peripheral facial palsy is Bell palsy, even though that is the most common cause; check the red-flag list before labeling it idiopathic.
boardTraps.quote: Bell palsy is by far the most common cause of unilateral peripheral facial nerve paralysis, not every peripheral facial palsy is the result of Bell palsy

boardTraps.text: A brainstem lesion can cause facial paresis with taste and tearing preserved, because the motor fibers are anatomically separate from the sensory-parasympathetic components.
boardTraps.quote: brainstem lesions may produce facial paresis with sparing of taste and tearing due to the anatomic separation of the motor fibers from the sensory-parasympathetic components

boardTraps.text: Aberrant regeneration after a peripheral palsy can cause crocodile tears (Bogorad syndrome) on the paretic side.
boardTraps.quote: aberrant regeneration may result in involuntary tearing of the eye on the involved paretic side (crocodile-tears or Bogorad syndrome)

boardTraps.text: In facial palsy, resting upper eyelid position and gentle closure are unaffected; blinking and tight closure are what fail.
boardTraps.quote: in cases of facial nerve palsy, the position of the upper eyelid, gentle closure of the eye, and lid-eye coordination are unaffected

11.title: Cranial Nerve VIII (The Vestibulocochlear Nerve)
11.subtitle: Separate conductive from sensorineural deafness and peripheral from central vertigo

points.text: Cochlear nerve fibers synapse in the cochlear nuclei; these second-order neurons send information to the contralateral brainstem via the lateral lemniscus.
points.quote: The dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei contain the second-order neurons of the auditory pathway and carry information to the contralateral brainstem, as the lateral lemniscus

points.text: The pathway has many commissural connections but none at the medial geniculate nucleus, so the representation is bilateral above the cochlear nuclei; this matters for unilateral brainstem lesions.
points.quote: Although many commissural connections exist along the auditory pathway, none exist at the level of the medial geniculate nucleus.

points.text: Primary auditory cortex is Brodmann area 41 in Heschl's transverse temporal gyrus.
points.quote: Most fibers end in lamina IV of the primary auditory cortex (AI, Brodmann area 41), in the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl

points.text: The cochlea and auditory brainstem nuclei are supplied by the internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery from AICA.
points.quote: Blood supply to the cochlea and auditory brainstem nuclei arise from the internal auditory artery (labyrinthine artery), a branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA).

points.text: The superior division of the vestibular nerve carries the anterior and horizontal canals and the utricle; the inferior division carries the posterior canal and saccule.
points.quote: The superior aspect of the vestibular nerve carries input from the anterior and horizontal semicircular canals and from the utricle

points.text: The vestibular nuclei serve stable vision during head movement and stable posture during body movement.
points.quote: These nuclei help to maintain stable vision during head movements and a stable posture during body movements

points.text: Only the superior vestibular nucleus projects to the ipsilateral MLF; the other nuclei project to the contralateral MLF.
points.quote: Although all the vestibular nuclei contribute to the MLF, only the superior vestibular nucleus projects to the ipsilateral MLF

points.text: The lateral vestibulospinal tract is ipsilateral and drives antigravity extensor tone.
points.quote: The lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVT) originates primarily from the lateral and inferior vestibular nuclei and projects to the ipsilateral spinal cord.

points.text: The anterior and posterior vestibular arteries map onto the superior and inferior divisions of the vestibular nerve.
points.quote: Thus, the anterior and posterior vestibular arteries carry blood flow to structures innervated by the superior and inferior branches of the vestibular nerve, respectively

localizationRules.explanation: Compare which ear hears the midline fork louder; it lateralizes to the deaf ear in conductive loss and to the normal ear in SNHL.
localizationRules.quote: In cases of conductive hearing loss, vibrations are recognized louder in the deaf ear (lateralization to the affected ear).

localizationRules.explanation: Air conduction stays better than bone conduction in SNHL (Rinne positive); in conductive loss bone conduction is better.
localizationRules.quote: With SNHL, both air and bone conduction are equally decreased, with air conduction remaining greater than bone conduction.

localizationRules.explanation: Because the ascending tracts above the cochlear nuclei are bilateral, a unilateral brainstem lesion seldom impairs hearing; hearing loss from the brainstem needs bilateral destructive lesions.
localizationRules.quote: Due to the binaural representation of the ascending auditory tracts rostral to the cochlear nuclei, brainstem lesions involving the auditory pathways seldom result in hearing impairment.

localizationRules.explanation: Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-rotatory and suppressed by fixation; vertical or purely rotatory nystagmus, or nystagmus not suppressed by fixation, points central.
localizationRules.quote: horizontal rotatory (never vertical or exclusively rotatory), and inhibited by visual fixation.

localizationRules.explanation: A central syndrome is more protracted and comes with brainstem or cerebellar signs; auditory symptoms are infrequent.
localizationRules.quote: Unlike the peripheral vestibular syndrome, the central vestibular syndrome is often more protracted, and signs of brainstem and cerebellar dysfunction are usually present.

localizationRules.explanation: Peripheral positional nystagmus is torsional, geotropic and fatigable after a latency; the book lists features that make a central cause likely (for example nystagmus that does not fatigue).
localizationRules.quote: The nystagmus is typically torsional, geotropic, and fatigable, often abating within 10 seconds from onset.

keySyndromes.name: Vestibular schwannoma (cerebellopontine angle)
keySyndromes.triad: Insidious progressive unilateral SNHL + Poor speech discrimination + Tinnitus
keySyndromes.clue: Imbalance is more frequent than vertigo; growth then adds trigeminal, abducens, facial and lower cranial nerve signs and cerebellar compromise.
keySyndromes.quote: Vestibular schwannomas usually result in insidious and progressive unilateral SNHL associated with poor speech discrimination and tinnitus.

keySyndromes.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
keySyndromes.triad: Brief attacks of acute severe vertigo + Nystagmus + Autonomic symptoms, triggered by head movements
keySyndromes.clue: Cochlear symptoms are typically absent; most often the posterior semicircular canal is involved.
keySyndromes.quote: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a common inner ear disorder characterized by brief attacks of acute and severe vertigo associated with nystagmus and autonomic symptoms.

keySyndromes.name: Vestibular neuronitis
keySyndromes.triad: Sudden severe prolonged vertigo + Spontaneous horizontal-rotatory nystagmus + Nausea and vomiting + Impaired caloric response
keySyndromes.clue: No hearing loss; acute labyrinthitis resembles it except for tinnitus and hearing loss.
keySyndromes.quote: sudden severe attacks of prolonged vertigo, spontaneous horizontal-rotatory nystagmus, nausea, vomiting, and impaired vestibular function on caloric testing

keySyndromes.name: Meniere disease
keySyndromes.triad: Episodic disabling vertigo + Fluctuating SNHL + Tinnitus
keySyndromes.clue: Early hearing loss affects low frequencies and fluctuates; aural fullness is common.
keySyndromes.quote: characterized by episodic acute and disabling attacks of vertigo, fluctuating SNHL, and tinnitus

keySyndromes.name: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary infarction)
keySyndromes.triad: Vertigo with illusion of tilting + Ipsilateral limb ataxia + Ipsilateral facial hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia + Pharyngeal paresis + Horner syndrome + Contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia
keySyndromes.clue: Nystagmus results from involvement of the ipsilateral vestibular nuclei.
keySyndromes.quote: ipsilateral limb ataxia, facial hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia, paresis of pharyngeal muscles, Horner syndrome, and contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia.

keySyndromes.name: Pure word deafness (auditory verbal agnosia)
keySyndromes.triad: Cannot understand spoken language + Normal auditory acuity + Reading, writing and naming preserved
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral temporal lesions affecting Heschl gyri or a unilateral dominant posterior temporal lesion; nonlanguage sounds are still understood.
keySyndromes.quote: bilateral temporal lobe lesions affecting Heschl gyri may result in pure word deafness, also known as auditory verbal agnosia

boardTraps.text: Vertebrobasilar ischemia can present as vertigo and dizziness that look like an acute peripheral vestibulopathy.
boardTraps.quote: Not infrequently, vertebrobasilar ischemia results in vertigo and dizziness, thus mimicking an acute peripheral vestibulopathy

boardTraps.text: Skew deviation points to brainstem involvement, even when an abnormal horizontal HIT falsely suggests a peripheral lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Skew deviation, a vertical misalignment of the two eyes caused by a supranuclear lesion, is also a good predictor of brainstem involvement

boardTraps.text: Infarction of the cerebellar nodulus can cause isolated vertigo that mimics vestibular neuritis.
boardTraps.quote: Isolated vertigo is an unusual manifestation of infarction of the cerebellar nodulus that may mimic an acute vestibular neuritis

boardTraps.text: Acute labyrinthitis versus vestibular neuronitis: the difference is auditory symptoms.
boardTraps.quote: It resembles vestibular neuronitis except for the associated tinnitus and hearing loss.

boardTraps.text: Auditory cortex lesions seldom cause obvious hearing loss; unilateral lesions more often disturb sound localization.
boardTraps.quote: A subtle hearing impairment may be seen with unilateral lesions, but more often these lesions impair sound localization.

boardTraps.text: With vestibular schwannoma, expect unsteadiness more than true vertigo.
boardTraps.quote: Imbalance, unsteadiness, or disequilibrium is more frequent than vertigo.

12.title: Cranial Nerves IX and X (The Glossopharyngeal and Vagus Nerves)
12.subtitle: Localize palate, pharynx and larynx deficits from supranuclear to nuclear, jugular foramen and laryngeal nerve lesions

points.text: IX, X and XI leave the medulla together and share the jugular foramen, so lesions there rarely spare a single nerve.
points.quote: These three nerves then travel together through the jugular foramen.

points.text: IX motor fibers come from the rostral nucleus ambiguus and supply the stylopharyngeus.
points.quote: The motor fibers originate from the rostral nucleus ambiguus and innervate the stylopharyngeus muscle (a pharyngeal elevator)

points.text: IX carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue.
points.quote: The sensory fibers carried in the glossopharyngeal nerve include taste afferents, supplying the posterior third of the tongue and the pharynx

points.text: Parasympathetic IX fibers start in the inferior salivatory nucleus and end in the parotid gland, via the otic ganglion.
points.quote: The parasympathetic fibers carried in the glossopharyngeal nerve originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, located in the periventricular gray matter of the rostral medulla

points.text: Taste over the posterior third of the tongue can be tested and is lost on the side of a nerve lesion.
points.quote: The integrity of taste sensation may be tested over the posterior third of the tongue and is lost ipsilaterally with nerve lesions.

points.text: Vagal motor fibers arise from two nuclei: the dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic) and the nucleus ambiguus (striated muscle).
points.quote: The motor fibers carried in the vagus nerve arise from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the nucleus ambiguus.

points.text: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the striated muscles of palate, pharynx and larynx, with the exceptions of tensor veli palatini and stylopharyngeus.
points.quote: Fibers from this nucleus supply all of the striated musculature of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx except the tensor veli palatini (cranial nerve V)

points.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, which belongs to the superior laryngeal nerve.
points.quote: The recurrent laryngeal nerves then divide into anterior and posterior rami, which supply all of the muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid muscle

points.text: The vagus carries sensation from the concha of the ear (auricular branch) to the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
points.quote: Exteroceptive sensation from the concha of the ear is carried by the vagus (jugular ganglion) to terminate in the descending (spinal) nucleus

points.text: The afferent limb of the gag reflex is IX; the efferent limb uses both IX and X.
points.quote: The afferent limb of the pharyngeal reflex (gag reflex) runs in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the efferent limb runs in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

localizationRules.explanation: Expect combined IX and X findings; look at neighbouring structures to place the lesion.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions affecting the glossopharyngeal nerve also usually involve the vagus, and syndromes affecting both nerves are therefore much more common

localizationRules.explanation: A single cortical or corticobulbar lesion does not produce a deficit because the nucleus ambiguus has bilateral input.
localizationRules.quote: Supranuclear lesions, if unilateral, do not result in any neurologic deficit because of bilateral corticobulbar input to the nucleus ambiguus.

localizationRules.explanation: These involve neighbouring cranial nerves and brainstem structures, so localize by the accompanying signs (for example Wallenberg syndrome).
localizationRules.quote: Such lesions commonly involve other cranial nerves, especially the vagus, and other brainstem structures (e.g., Wallenberg syndrome)

localizationRules.explanation: On phonation the weak side fails to rise and the uvula is pulled toward the normal side.
localizationRules.quote: with phonation, the ipsilateral palate fails to elevate, and the uvula is retracted toward the nonparalyzed side

localizationRules.rule: Gag reflex in a vagal lesion
localizationRules.explanation: A unilateral vagal lesion depresses the gag reflex on its own side because it breaks the efferent limb.
localizationRules.quote: Therefore, unilateral vagal lesions depress the ipsilateral gag reflex by interrupting the efferent arc.

keySyndromes.name: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid paresis and atrophy (XI) + Dysphonia, dysphagia, depressed gag reflex, palatal droop and homolateral vocal cord paralysis (IX, X) + Loss of taste and anesthesia of the posterior third of the tongue, soft palate, pharynx and larynx + Often dull aching pain behind the ear
keySyndromes.clue: IX, X and XI together; the hypoglossal nerve is spared (compare Collet-Sicard).
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions at the jugular foramen, especially glomus jugulare tumors and basal skull fractures, injure cranial nerves IX, X, and XI

keySyndromes.name: Collet-Sicard syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Palsy of cranial nerves IX + X + XI + XII
keySyndromes.clue: Seen with retropharyngeal or retroparotid space lesions; Villaret syndrome adds the sympathetic chain and occasionally cranial nerve VII.
keySyndromes.quote: Resulting syndromes include the Collet-Sicard syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII)

keySyndromes.name: Avellis syndrome (palatopharyngeal paralysis)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral palatal paralysis + Ipsilateral pharyngeal paralysis + Laryngeal function spared
keySyndromes.clue: A lesion confined to the more cephalad nucleus ambiguus, owing to its somatotopic organization.
keySyndromes.quote: When only the more cephalad portion of the nucleus ambiguus is injured, laryngeal function is spared (palatopharyngeal paralysis of Avellis)

keySyndromes.name: Glossopharyngeal (vagoglossopharyngeal) neuralgia
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral stabbing paroxysmal pain in throat or ear + Lasting seconds to minutes + Triggered by chewing, coughing, talking, yawning or swallowing
keySyndromes.clue: No neurologic deficit in the primary form; attacks may bring syncope through reflex bradycardia and asystole.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a unilateral pain (usually stabbing, sharp, and paroxysmal) located in the field of sensory distribution of the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerves

keySyndromes.name: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
keySyndromes.triad: Hoarseness, often transient + Flaccid dysphonia with breathiness and mild inhalatory stridor + Paralyzed vocal cord near the midline + Palatopharyngeal function normal
keySyndromes.clue: Cricothyroid is spared because the superior laryngeal nerve supplies it; the left nerve is injured more often.
keySyndromes.quote: With unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, unilateral paralysis of all laryngeal muscles (except the cricothyroid, which is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve) occurs.

keySyndromes.name: Syncope from glossopharyngeal or vagal metastasis
keySyndromes.triad: Severe paroxysms of pain in neck, ear or side of head + Syncope from sudden hypotension + Sometimes bradycardia
keySyndromes.clue: Typically in head and neck cancer, especially when the tumor recurs after treatment; may be the only symptom.
keySyndromes.quote: Syncope with or without pain may be the only symptom of metastatic involvement of the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerve

boardTraps.text: In pseudobulbar states the gag reflex can be depressed or exaggerated, so its presence does not exclude bilateral corticobulbar disease.
boardTraps.quote: With stimulation, the gag reflex may be depressed or markedly exaggerated, resulting in severe retching and even vomiting.

boardTraps.text: An isolated IX lesion is subtle: motor weakness may be negligible, with at most mild dysphagia.
boardTraps.quote: Motor paresis may be negligible with glossopharyngeal nerve lesions, although mild dysphagia may occur

boardTraps.text: A superior laryngeal nerve lesion causes few findings because the nerve is mainly sensory; the cricothyroid is the only motor target.
boardTraps.quote: Lesions of this nerve result in few clinical findings because this branch is primarily sensory.

boardTraps.text: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer and is injured more often than the right.
boardTraps.quote: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right and is therefore damaged more often.

boardTraps.text: A unilateral vagal lesion leaves the vocal cord in the cadaveric position and, despite impaired voluntary cough, causes little dyspnea.
boardTraps.quote: The ipsilateral vocal cord assumes the cadaveric position (midway between adduction and abduction), and although voluntary coughing may be impaired, there is little dyspnea.

boardTraps.text: Unlike trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia is very rarely caused by multiple sclerosis.
boardTraps.quote: Multiple sclerosis is an extremely rare etiology for this syndrome

13.title: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
13.subtitle: Localize weakness of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius from cortex to neck, and recognize the jugular foramen and lower cranial nerve syndromes

points.text: The cranial (internal) root comes from the caudal nucleus ambiguus and travels with the vagus to supply pharynx and larynx.
points.quote: The cranial root arises from cells situated in the caudal part of the nucleus ambiguus of the medulla.

points.text: The spinal root is somatotopic: upper cervical segments serve mainly the sternocleidomastoid and C3-C4 serve mainly the trapezius, which explains why the two muscles can be affected separately.
points.quote: cord levels C1 and C2 innervate predominantly the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle, and levels C3 and C4 innervate primarily the ipsilateral trapezius

points.text: Cranial and spinal roots join and leave the skull together through the jugular foramen, so skull-base lesions rarely spare neighbouring nerves.
points.quote: The cranial and spinal roots unite and exit from the skull through the jugular foramen.

points.text: Corticobulbar input to the trapezius is crossed, so each hemisphere drives the contralateral trapezius.
points.quote: The corticobulbar fibers to the trapezius are crossed, and thus one cerebral hemisphere supplies the contralateral trapezius muscle.

points.text: The sternocleidomastoid pathway is not well defined; it is thought to end mainly in the ipsilateral nuclei, with several alternative routes proposed.
points.quote: The course of the fibers controlling the sternocleidomastoid muscle is unknown, but the fibers are thought to terminate chiefly in the ipsilateral nuclei.

points.text: Sternocleidomastoid fibers run in the brainstem tegmentum and trapezius fibers run ventrally, which allows dissociated brainstem patterns.
points.quote: The corticobulbar fibers to the sternocleidomastoid are located in the brainstem tegmentum, whereas fibers to the trapezius are located in the ventral brainstem

points.text: A ventral pontine lesion can therefore weaken the trapezius supranuclearly while the sternocleidomastoid is spared.
points.quote: Thus, a ventral pontine lesion can cause supranuclear paresis of the trapezius with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

points.text: Each sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side, so the right muscle is tested by turning the head to the left against resistance.
points.quote: The right sternocleidomastoid is thus tested by having the patient rotate his or her head to the left against resistance

points.text: The trapezius is tested with a bilateral shoulder shrug against resistance, comparing the two sides by looking and palpating.
points.quote: muscle is tested by having the patient shrug his or her shoulders against resistance and comparing the two sides by observation and palpation.

localizationRules.explanation: Head position at rest is normal; the deficit is weak turning of the head to the opposite side, and on flexion the head drifts toward the unaffected side because the other muscle is unopposed.
localizationRules.quote: There is weakness in turning the head to the opposite side, and when the patient flexes the head, it rotates slightly

localizationRules.explanation: Look for a low shoulder at rest and a displaced, slightly winged scapula; the upper fibers are mainly affected in nerve XI lesions.
localizationRules.quote: The shoulder is lower on the affected side at rest, and the scapula is displaced downward and laterally with its vertebral border slightly winged.

localizationRules.explanation: Bilateral trapezius weakness weakens neck extension (head falls forward), whereas bilateral sternocleidomastoid weakness weakens neck flexion (head tends to fall backward).
localizationRules.quote: Bilateral trapezius paresis results in weakness of neck extension, with the head tending to fall forward when the patient attempts to stand erect.

localizationRules.explanation: With a hemispheric lesion causing contralateral hemiplegia, the trapezius is weak on the hemiplegic side but the weak sternocleidomastoid is on the side of the cerebral lesion, so the head turns away from the hemiplegic side.
localizationRules.quote: the head is turned away from the hemiplegic side, indicating paresis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the side opposite the hemiplegia

localizationRules.rule: Geschwind rule for hemiplegia plus sternocleidomastoid paresis
localizationRules.explanation: Compare the side of the weak sternocleidomastoid with the hemiplegic side: if opposite, think hemisphere; if the same side, the lesion is at or below the pons.
localizationRules.quote: hemiplegia associated with ipsilateral (to the hemiplegia) sternocleidomastoid paresis implies a lesion at or below the pontine level

keySyndromes.name: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid paresis and atrophy + dysphonia and dysphagia with depressed gag reflex, palatal droop and vocal cord paralysis + loss of taste and depressed sensation over the posterior third of the tongue, soft palate, pharynx and larynx
keySyndromes.clue: Involves IX, X and XI together; adding tongue paralysis (XII) moves the picture to Collet-Sicard.
keySyndromes.quote: The spinal accessory nerve enters the jugular foramen accompanied by cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal nerve) and cranial nerve X (vagus nerve).

keySyndromes.name: Collet-Sicard syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Paralysis of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid (XI) + paralysis of the vocal cord (X) and pharynx (IX) + hemiparalysis of the tongue (XII) + loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue (IX) + hemianesthesia of the palate, pharynx and larynx (IX, X)
keySyndromes.clue: All four lower cranial nerves IX to XII on one side; all findings are ipsilateral to the lesion, often in the retroparotid space.
keySyndromes.quote: Involvement of all four of the lower cranial nerves (IX through XII) results in the Collet-Sicard

keySyndromes.name: Villaret syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Cranial nerves IX + X + XI + XII + cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral Horner syndrome) + occasionally VII
keySyndromes.clue: Like Collet-Sicard but with sympathetic involvement; located in the retroparotid or retropharyngeal space.
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions of the retroparotid or retropharyngeal spaces may cause Villaret syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, the sympathetic chain

keySyndromes.name: Trapezius weak, sternocleidomastoid spared
keySyndromes.triad: Weakness of the trapezius on one side + sparing of the sternocleidomastoid
keySyndromes.clue: Points to a ventral brainstem lesion, a lower cervical cord lesion, or a lower spinal accessory root lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: Weakness of the trapezius on one side with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid muscles indicates a ventral brainstem lesion

keySyndromes.name: Sternocleidomastoid weak, trapezius spared
keySyndromes.triad: Weakness of the sternocleidomastoid + trapezius sparing
keySyndromes.clue: Points to a lower brainstem tegmentum lesion or to upper cervical accessory roots.
keySyndromes.quote: Weakness of the sternocleidomastoid with trapezius sparing indicates a lesion of the lower brainstem tegmentum

keySyndromes.name: Nuclear lesions of the accessory nucleus
keySyndromes.triad: Paresis of trapezius and sternocleidomastoid + prominent atrophy + fasciculations
keySyndromes.clue: Rare; suggested by associated medullary or upper cervical cord dysfunction (motor neuron disease, intraparenchymal tumor, syringomyelia).
keySyndromes.quote: These relatively rare lesions result in paresis with prominent atrophy and fasciculations that affect the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

boardTraps.text: Dissociated weakness (trapezius weak on one side, sternocleidomastoid weak on the other) indicates an upper motor neuron lesion ipsilateral to the weak sternocleidomastoid and above the oculomotor complex.
boardTraps.quote: Weakness of the trapezius on one side associated with weakness of the sternocleidomastoid on the other (dissociated weakness) indicates an upper motor neuron lesion

boardTraps.text: Medullary lesions affecting corticobulbar fibers weaken head turning toward the lesion, the opposite of the cortical, capsular and high brainstem pattern.
boardTraps.quote: Thus, medullary lesions affecting corticobulbar fibers may result in decreased strength on the head turning toward the lesion

boardTraps.text: Nerve XI lesions do not cause sensory disturbance, so sensory loss in a jugular foramen syndrome has to come from neighbouring nerves such as IX and X.
boardTraps.quote: Because the spinal accessory nerve is a purely motor nerve (except for some proprioceptive afferent fibers), nerve lesions do not result in sensory disturbance.

boardTraps.text: In nerve XI lesions the trapezius weakness affects predominantly the upper fibers, the part not supplied by the cervical plexus.
boardTraps.quote: Unilateral trapezius paresis due to spinal accessory nerve lesions affects predominantly the upper trapezius fibers (the part not supplied by the cervical plexus).

boardTraps.text: A traction injury in the posterior cervical triangle, distal to the sternocleidomastoid, gives isolated trapezius weakness; the nerve is vulnerable to iatrogenic injury there, for example at lymph node biopsy.
boardTraps.quote: With injuries (e.g., traction) in the posterior cervical triangle distal to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, trapezius weakness occurs in isolation

boardTraps.text: Dropped (floppy) head is not a nerve XI sign by default: the book lists many central, neuropathic, neuromuscular junction, myopathic and mechanical causes in Table 13-2.
boardTraps.quote: Weakness of neck extension against gravity with or without involvement of neck flexion has been called the floppy head syndrome

14.title: Cranial Nerve XII (The Hypoglossal Nerve)
14.subtitle: Tell supranuclear from nuclear and peripheral tongue weakness and place the lesion from medulla to skull base to neck

points.text: The hypoglossal nucleus is a paramedian medullary column under the floor of the fourth ventricle.
points.quote: a longitudinal cell column in the paramedian medulla that lies beneath the hypoglossal trigone of the floor of the fourth ventricle

points.text: Rootlets leave the medulla between olive and pyramid, so intramedullary lesions near the pyramid can involve the nerve.
points.quote: The fibers of the hypoglossal nerve emerge from the medulla in the preolivary sulcus between the inferior olivary complex and the pyramid

points.text: The nerve exits the skull in the hypoglossal canal and descends in the neck close to the carotid artery and jugular vein.
points.quote: After leaving the skull in the hypoglossal canal (anterior condylar foramen), the two nerve bundles unite and descend vertically through the neck

points.text: The nerve supplies all intrinsic tongue muscles plus the extrinsic hyoglossus, styloglossus, genioglossus and geniohyoid.
points.quote: The hypoglossal muscular or lingual branches supply all the intrinsic muscles of the tongue (longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles)

points.text: Only the genioglossus has crossed corticobulbar control; the other tongue muscles are bilaterally controlled.
points.quote: The corticobulbar fibers controlling the genioglossus muscles are crossed; the other tongue muscles appear to have bilateral supranuclear control.

points.text: Corticohypoglossal fibers cross at the pontomedullary junction and reach the nucleus from its lateral side.
points.quote: Cortical projections to the hypoglossal nucleus cross the midline in the pontomedullary junction and enter the hypoglossal nucleus from its lateral aspect

localizationRules.explanation: A lower motor neuron lesion gives a wasted, twitching half tongue on the same side as the lesion.
localizationRules.quote: Unilateral lesions of the hypoglossal nerve result in paresis, atrophy, furrowing, fibrillations, and fasciculations that affect the corresponding half of the tongue.

localizationRules.explanation: On protrusion the tongue deviates to the weak side because the normal genioglossus pushes unopposed.
localizationRules.quote: during which the tongue deviates to the side of paresis, mainly because of the unopposed action of the normal contralateral genioglossus muscle

localizationRules.explanation: If the tongue is weak but not atrophic and without fibrillations, think of a corticobulbar lesion rather than a nuclear or nerve lesion.
localizationRules.quote: A supranuclear lesion is not accompanied by atrophy or fibrillations of the tongue.

localizationRules.explanation: Because genioglossus control comes mainly from the contralateral cortex, a lesion above the crossing weakens the contralateral half of the tongue.
localizationRules.quote: a lesion of the corticobulbar fibers above their decussation may result in weakness of the contralateral half of the tongue

localizationRules.explanation: Look for neighbouring long-tract signs to place a hypoglossal lesion inside the medulla.
localizationRules.quote: Intramedullary hypoglossal involvement is suggested by the associated affection of the medial lemniscus, pyramid, or other neighboring intramedullary structures.

keySyndromes.name: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine anterior bulbar)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral tongue paresis, atrophy and fibrillations (tongue deviates toward the lesion) + contralateral hemiplegia with sparing of the face + contralateral loss of position and vibratory sensation
keySyndromes.clue: Pain and temperature are spared because the more dorsolateral spinothalamic tract is unaffected.
keySyndromes.quote: This syndrome results from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or its parent vertebral artery.

keySyndromes.name: Collet-Sicard syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Paralysis of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid (XI) + paralysis of the vocal cord (X) and pharynx (IX) + hemiparalysis of the tongue (XII) + loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue (IX) + hemianesthesia of the palate, pharynx and larynx (IX, X)
keySyndromes.clue: Lower cranial nerves IX to XII damaged together at the skull base, for example by a fracture through the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen.
keySyndromes.quote: When all four of these nerves are damaged (e.g., by a skull fracture through the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen), a Collet-Sicard syndrome results

keySyndromes.name: Villaret syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Cranial nerves IX + X + XI + XII + cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral Horner syndrome) + occasionally VII
keySyndromes.clue: Retroparotid or retropharyngeal space; the sympathetic involvement separates it from Collet-Sicard.
keySyndromes.quote: For example, lesions of the retroparotid or retropharyngeal spaces may cause Villaret syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII

keySyndromes.name: Occipital condyle syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Continuous severe unilateral occipital pain worse with neck flexion + neck stiffness + ipsilateral tongue weakness and atrophy, with the protruded tongue deviating to the involved side
keySyndromes.clue: Rotating the head toward the painful side often relieves the pain, whereas rotation to the nonpainful side is unbearable.
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions, usually tumors or chronic inflammatory lesions, of the occipital condyle may cause occipital pain associated with an ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve injury

keySyndromes.name: Combined abducens and hypoglossal palsies
keySyndromes.triad: Abducens nerve palsy + hypoglossal nerve palsy
keySyndromes.clue: Usually localizes to the clivus and is often ominous (nasopharyngeal carcinoma is Godtfredsen syndrome), but lower brainstem and subarachnoid processes can do it too.
keySyndromes.quote: Although the combination of abducens nerve palsy with a hypoglossal nerve palsy usually localizes the pathologic process to the clivus

keySyndromes.name: Tapia syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve injury + recurrent laryngeal nerve (vagus branch) injury
keySyndromes.clue: Reported after otolaryngologic or cervical spine surgery, endotracheal anesthesia and prolonged ventilation.
keySyndromes.quote: resulting from injury to the ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve and recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve, has been reported following otolaryngologic surgery

boardTraps.text: Tongue deviation depends on the level: nerve and nuclear lesions deviate toward the weak side, while an internal capsule lesion may deviate the tongue toward the side of the hemiplegia.
boardTraps.quote: Also, with an internal capsular lesion, the tongue may deviate toward the side of the hemiplegia.

boardTraps.text: A cortical lesion can mimic a peripheral hypoglossal palsy with the tongue deviating away from the lesion, but without atrophy or fibrillations.
boardTraps.quote: A lesion of the precentral and postcentral gyri may thus cause a contralateral supranuclear hypoglossal palsy

boardTraps.text: The crossing of corticohypoglossal fibers is not absolute: ipsilateral supranuclear tongue weakness has been described with a pontine infarct, and a contralateral glossoplegia with an upper medullary lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Indeed, ipsilateral lingual paresis has been described due to pontine infarct

boardTraps.text: The hypoglossal fibers lie somewhat lateral to the lemniscus and pyramid, so in anterior spinal artery occlusion the tongue is occasionally spared.
boardTraps.quote: Because the hypoglossal fibers run somewhat laterally to the medial lemniscus and pyramid, they are occasionally spared in cases of anterior spinal artery occlusion.

boardTraps.text: Unilateral tongue lesions cause little dysarthria or dysphagia; the main complaint is trouble moving food in the mouth, whereas bilateral lesions make dysphagia prominent.
boardTraps.quote: With unilateral lesions, dysarthria and dysphagia are minimal, but difficulty with manipulating food in the mouth is often evident.

boardTraps.text: In one reported patient, protrusion (extrinsic muscles) and sideways movement of the non-protruded tongue (intrinsic muscles) were dissociated, so testing both may help separate extrinsic from intrinsic weakness.
boardTraps.quote: protrusion of the tongue requires the action of extrinsic tongue muscles, whereas lateral movements of the nonprotruded tongue are accomplished by intrinsic muscles

16.title: The Cerebellum
16.subtitle: Localize cerebellar signs to midline, intermediate or lateral zones and recognize the PICA, AICA and SCA infarct syndromes

points.text: The primary fissure separates anterior from posterior lobe; the flocculonodular lobe is the third, separate lobe.
points.quote: The anterior lobe is separated from the posterior lobe by the primary fissure

points.text: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) links to the vestibular system and eye movements.
points.quote: The vestibulocerebellum corresponds to the flocculonodular lobe and has rich connections with the vestibular system and with brain areas concerned with eye movements

points.text: The spinocerebellum receives mainly spinal input and modulates tone, axial and limb movements.
points.quote: The spinocerebellum receives input mainly from the spinal cord and plays a major role in the modulation of muscle tone

points.text: The cerebrocerebellum (middle vermis and most of the hemispheres) plans and coordinates ipsilateral fine limb movements.
points.quote: major role in planning and initiation of movements, as well as the regulation and coordination of ipsilateral fine limb

points.text: The deep nuclei, from medial to lateral, are fastigial, interpositus (emboliform plus globose) and dentate.
points.quote: From medial to lateral, these nuclei are the fastigial nucleus, the nucleus interpositus (formed by the emboliform and globose nuclei), and the dentate nucleus.

points.text: The fastigial nucleus is tied to stance and gait, which matches the midline syndrome of truncal and gait ataxia.
points.quote: The fastigial nucleus is involved with stance and gait

points.text: The middle peduncle is purely afferent, while the inferior and superior peduncles carry both afferent and efferent tracts.
points.quote: The inferior and superior cerebellar peduncles carry afferent and efferent tracts; the middle cerebellar peduncle is exclusively afferent.

points.text: Dentate output through the superior peduncle goes to the contralateral ventrolateral thalamus.
points.quote: The dentatothalamic tract, which transmits output to the contralateral ventrolateral nucleus of the thalamus.

points.text: PICA supplies the inferior half of the cerebellum and also the lateral medullary tegmentum and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
points.quote: supplies the half of the cerebellum below the plane of the great horizontal fissure, encompassing the lateral medullary tegmentum, inferior cerebellar peduncle

points.text: AICA supplies the anterior petrosal surface, flocculus, lower middle peduncle and lateral pontomedullary tegmentum.
points.quote: supplies the anterior petrosal surface of the cerebellar hemisphere, the flocculus, lower portion of the middle cerebellar peduncle, and lateral pontomedullary tegmentum

points.text: SCA supplies the upper surface of the hemisphere, the superior vermis and most of the dentate nucleus, along with the superior peduncle and lateral pontine tegmentum.
points.quote: supplies the upper surface of the cerebellar hemisphere, ipsilateral portion of the superior vermis, most of the dentate nucleus

localizationRules.explanation: Trunk and balance problems point to the midline; fine limb incoordination on the same side points to a hemisphere.
localizationRules.quote: In general, disorders mainly involving the midline cerebellum affect the truncal musculature and equilibrium.

localizationRules.explanation: Stance and gait disorder, truncal titubation and eye movement disturbance localize to vermis, fastigial nucleus and their projections.
localizationRules.quote: cerebellar signs resulting from midline cerebellar disease are characterized by disorders of stance and gait, truncal titubation

localizationRules.explanation: The hemisphere and dentate nucleus cause ipsilateral limb signs plus hypotonia and dysarthria.
localizationRules.quote: lesions of the lateral zone result in hypotonia, dysarthria, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, excessive rebound, impaired check response, kinetic and static tremors

localizationRules.explanation: Closing the eyes does not unmask cerebellar ataxia, whereas sensory ataxia gets clearly worse.
localizationRules.quote: Cerebellar ataxia characteristically persists in spite of visual cues (unlike sensory ataxia, which is more pronounced with eyes closed).

localizationRules.explanation: Hypotonia after an acute hemispheric lesion is on the same side as the damage and most noticeable in proximal arm segments.
localizationRules.quote: The hypotonia is ipsilateral to the side of cerebellar damage and more noticeable in proximal segments of the upper limbs.

keySyndromes.name: Rostral vermis syndrome (anterior lobe)
keySyndromes.triad: Wide-based stance and titubating gait + gait ataxia with proportionally minimal ataxia on heel-to-shin testing supine + normal or only slightly impaired coordination of the upper extremities
keySyndromes.clue: Hypotonia, nystagmus and dysarthria are infrequent; classic example is alcoholic cerebellar cortical degeneration.
