keySyndromes.quote: The rostral vermis syndrome is best exemplified by the restricted form of alcoholic cerebellar cortical degeneration

keySyndromes.name: Caudal vermis syndrome (flocculonodular and posterior lobe)
keySyndromes.triad: Axial disequilibrium and staggering gait + mild or no limb ataxia + occasional spontaneous nystagmus and rotated head postures
keySyndromes.clue: Typical of flocculonodular damage, especially medulloblastoma in children.
keySyndromes.quote: This caudal vermis syndrome is typically observed with flocculonodular lobe damage, especially with medulloblastomas in children.

keySyndromes.name: Hemispheric syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Incoordination of ipsilateral appendicular movements + worst for tasks needing fine motor coordination (finger movements, speech)
keySyndromes.clue: Usually from cerebellar strokes, neoplasms or abscesses.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with this syndrome typically show incoordination of ipsilateral appendicular movements, particularly when the tasks require fine motor coordination.

keySyndromes.name: PICA territory infarction
keySyndromes.triad: Medial PICA: acute vertigo + truncal ataxia; lateral PICA: unsteadiness + limb ataxia + dysmetria without dysarthria
keySyndromes.clue: Most symptomatic cerebellar infarctions are PICA territory, often from occlusion of the intracranial vertebral artery before the PICA origin.
keySyndromes.quote: lateral PICA territory infarctions result in unsteadiness, limb ataxia, and dysmetria without associated dysarthria

keySyndromes.name: AICA territory infarction
keySyndromes.triad: Prominent vertigo, nausea, vomiting and nystagmus + ipsilateral facial hypalgesia, thermoanesthesia and corneal hypesthesia + ipsilateral Horner syndrome + contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia + ipsilateral ataxia and asynergia + ipsilateral deafness and facial paralysis
keySyndromes.clue: Facial palsy, deafness and lateral gaze palsy favor AICA over lateral medullary syndrome.
keySyndromes.quote: facial palsy and deafness due to involvement of cranial nerves VII and VIII or their nuclei, lateral gaze palsy

keySyndromes.name: SCA territory infarction
keySyndromes.triad: Vertigo and vomiting + nystagmus + ipsilateral Horner syndrome + ipsilateral ataxia, asynergia and intention tremor + contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia + contralateral hearing impairment + contralateral fourth nerve palsy
keySyndromes.clue: The book says this classic picture is seldom seen; occlusion of peripheral SCA branches often gives isolated dysarthria and unsteady gait.
keySyndromes.quote: Contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia (due to involvement of the lateral spinothalamic and quintothalamic tracts)

boardTraps.text: AICA infarction can be mistaken for a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome because they share dysmetria, vestibular signs, Horner syndrome and facial sensory loss with contralateral body pain and temperature loss.
boardTraps.quote: The AICA syndrome may at times be mistakenly attributed to a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome because of shared signs

boardTraps.text: Isolated hemiataxia is usually an ipsilateral cerebellar stroke, but a contralateral supratentorial stroke (thalamus extending into the posterior limb of the internal capsule, or the capsule alone) can also cause it.
boardTraps.quote: Acute onset of isolated hemiataxia is, in most cases, due to an ipsilateral cerebellar stroke.

boardTraps.text: Small border zone cerebellar infarcts can look like a peripheral vestibular problem, even with canal paresis.
boardTraps.quote: Small or border zone cerebellar infarctions may simulate acute vestibular neuritis, including canal paresis

boardTraps.text: Contrapulsion of saccades from a cerebellar (SCA) lesion goes contralateral to the lesion, unlike the ipsilateral lateropulsion of saccades in Wallenberg syndrome.
boardTraps.quote: This contrapulsion of saccades (lateropulsion contralateral to a cerebellar lesion) differs from the lateropulsion of saccades observed in the lateral medullary syndrome of Wallenberg

boardTraps.text: In large cerebellar infarcts, a drop in alertness may appear hours to days after onset, signalling brainstem compression; emergency surgery is often required.
boardTraps.quote: Impaired level of alertness may occur hours to days after the onset of symptoms, either in isolation or in association

boardTraps.text: Absence of motor signs does not exclude a cerebellar infarct, especially one involving lobule VI.
boardTraps.quote: Motor symptoms may be minimal or completely lacking, particularly among patients with infarctions involving lobule VI of the cerebellum

17.title: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Hypothalamus and Pituitary Gland
17.subtitle: Linking temperature, sleep, water, feeding and endocrine syndromes to hypothalamic and pituitary sites

points.text: The hypothalamus is the lateral wall of the third ventricle and is separated from the thalamus by the hypothalamic sulcus.
points.quote: It is separated from the thalamus by the hypothalamic sulcus.

points.text: The fornix pillar, running down to the mammillary body, splits the hypothalamus into medial and lateral regions.
points.quote: Each pillar of the fornix, descending rostrocaudally to end in the mammillary body, divides the hypothalamus into a medial and a lateral region.

points.text: For localization, a coronal plane through the infundibular stalk and an angled parasagittal plane through the fornix give four regions.
points.quote: These planes separate four regions: anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral.

points.text: Anterior pituitary secretion is controlled by hypophysiotropic (releasing) factors delivered through the infundibular portal system.
points.quote: The hormonal secretions of the anterior pituitary are regulated by the hypothalamic-releasing factors or hypophysiotropic hormones

points.text: Supraoptic and paraventricular neurons send axons through the infundibulum to the posterior lobe, where oxytocin and ADH are secreted.
points.quote: constituted by axons from neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei

points.text: The tuberoinfundibular dopamine system arises in the arcuate nucleus and reaches the median eminence; dopamine in the portal system inhibits prolactin release.
points.quote: the tuberoinfundibular dopamine system, arising in the arcuate nucleus and projecting to the median eminence

points.text: The hypothalamus is tied to the midbrain and posterior tegmentum (alertness), the limbic system (emotion and memory) and brainstem autonomic nuclei.
points.quote: the midbrain and posterior tegmentum, which play an important role in alertness

points.text: Hypothalamic influence on spinal autonomic centers is probably relayed mainly through the brainstem reticular formation, although direct connections to the intermediolateral column exist.
points.quote: much of the influence of the hypothalamus on the autonomic centers of the cord is probably exerted through the brainstem reticular formation

points.text: Retinal and olfactory pathways bring information used for circadian control of vegetative functions.
points.quote: Pathways from the retina and olfactory system convey to the hypothalamus information needed for the circadian control of vegetative functions

localizationRules.explanation: Anterior hypothalamic lesions give hyperthermia, whereas posterior lesions give hypothermia or poikilothermia.
localizationRules.quote: hyperthermia results from anterior hypothalamic lesions, whereas posterior lesions cause hypothermia or poikilothermia by interfering with heat-conservation responses

localizationRules.explanation: Several hypothalamic portions are often hit together, so fine localization from human lesions is often uncertain; unilateral lesions are seldom symptomatic.
localizationRules.quote: Because these structures are small, several portions may be involved simultaneously.

localizationRules.explanation: Fast lesions (surgical or vascular) produce more florid pictures than slowly growing ones affecting the same structures.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions that progress rapidly cause a more florid clinical symptomatology than those that proceed slowly.

localizationRules.explanation: Sympathetic areas lie ventromedial and posterior (stimulation gives hypertension and pupillary dilation); parasympathetic areas are paraventricular or lateral, and anterior.
localizationRules.quote: Sympathetic areas tend to be ventromedial and posterior. Stimulation of these areas causes hypertension, pupillary dilation,

localizationRules.explanation: A unilateral hypothalamic lesion may be revealed by an ipsilateral Horner syndrome with miosis.
localizationRules.quote: Unilateral hypothalamic lesions may betray their presence by causing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome with miosis.

keySyndromes.name: Central diabetes insipidus (supraoptic/paraventricular)
keySyndromes.triad: Lack of ADH preventing water reabsorption + Large volume of dilute urine + Intact thirst preventing hypernatremia
keySyndromes.clue: Thirst is preserved, unlike essential hypernatremia; often the tract rather than the cell bodies is damaged, so it is often transient.
keySyndromes.quote: Diabetes insipidus results from involvement of at least 90% of the large neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei

keySyndromes.name: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)
keySyndromes.triad: Serum hyposmolarity and hyponatremia + Normal renal excretion of sodium + Inappropriately high urine osmolality without body fluid depletion
keySyndromes.clue: Usually extrahypothalamic in cause; only partial damage of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei or neighboring areas may produce it.
keySyndromes.quote: Although SIADH is more often due to extrahypothalamic causes, partial damage of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei or neighboring areas may cause the syndrome.

keySyndromes.name: Ventromedial hypothalamic obesity
keySyndromes.triad: Hyperphagia until a higher body weight is reached + Stable body weight afterwards unless the lesion progresses
keySyndromes.clue: Obesity may reflect damage to catecholaminergic pathways crossing the region rather than to the nuclei themselves.
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions in the ventromedial portion of the hypothalamus may cause obesity

keySyndromes.name: Poikilothermia (posterior hypothalamus)
keySyndromes.triad: Body temperature fluctuating with ambient temperature + Unawareness of the condition + No discomfort or behavioral regulation under thermal stress
keySyndromes.clue: Described as the most common central neurogenic abnormality of heat regulation in humans; arises from posterior hypothalamic lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: Such patients are unaware of their condition and show no sign of discomfort or behavioral regulation with thermal stress.

keySyndromes.name: Hypothalamic hamartoma
keySyndromes.triad: Gelastic seizures + Precocious puberty + Executive function disorders
keySyndromes.clue: Hamartomas of the sessile or intrahypothalamic type at the level of the mammillary bodies are most often the cause of gelastic seizures.
keySyndromes.quote: Hypothalamic hamartoma, particularly of the sessile or intrahypothalamic type, at the level of the mammillary bodies

keySyndromes.name: Pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm
keySyndromes.triad: Bitemporal visual field defects + Headache + Hormonal excess or deficiency
keySyndromes.clue: Asymmetric growth may instead cause unilateral blindness or, via the optic tract, a homonymous hemianopia.
keySyndromes.quote: Bitemporal defects, related to compression of the inferior aspect of the chiasm, are most common.

boardTraps.text: The same hypothalamic lesion can cause different syndromes at different ages, for example dwarfism in childhood but gigantism in adulthood.
boardTraps.quote: For instance, a similar lesion may cause dwarfism during childhood and gigantism during adulthood

boardTraps.text: Pyrogen-induced hyperthermia is the most common cause; cases labeled hypothalamic hyperthermia after a negative infectious search often belong here, since pyrogens can act on the hypothalamus directly.
boardTraps.quote: Bacterial or viral pyrogens can stimulate directly the hypothalamus and, in addition, induce the release of interleukin 1

boardTraps.text: Malignant hyperthermia is covered with temperature disorders but is not hypothalamic in origin.
boardTraps.quote: Although not due to hypothalamic dysfunction, this syndrome is discussed here with other abnormalities of temperature control.

boardTraps.text: Serotonin syndrome resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome but with milder fever and more myoclonus, ocular clonus and hyperreflexia (Table 17-3: no rigidity, normal CPK).
boardTraps.quote: usually with milder fever and a greater tendency to develop myoclonus, ocular clonus, and hyperreflexia

boardTraps.text: Essential hypernatremia needs absent thirst with preserved conscious behavior, which separates it from diabetes insipidus where thirst is intact.
boardTraps.quote: impaired secretion of ADH with hypernatremia, and (4) the absence of thirst despite preserved conscious behavior

boardTraps.text: Diabetes insipidus is often transient when the lesion damages the supraopticohypophysial tract rather than the neuronal bodies (familial forms excepted).
boardTraps.quote: Except for the familial variety, the lesion often affects the supraopticohypophysial tract rather than the neuronal bodies themselves.

18.title: The Anatomic Localization of Lesions in the Thalamus
18.subtitle: Reading thalamic stroke syndromes by arterial territory and nuclear group

points.text: The thalamus is divided into anterior, posterior, medial and lateral regions, with the intralaminar nuclei in the core.
points.quote: four regions can be distinguished in the thalamus: anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral

points.text: Thalamic names only loosely match human position: the VL nucleus is also dorsal, reaching the highest thalamic level.
points.quote: the ventrolateral (VL) nucleus is not only ventral in humans, but extends to the highest level of the thalamus

points.text: Midline, intralaminar, reticular and some ventral anterior nuclei are the nonspecific nuclei that mediate cortical alerting.
points.quote: The midline, intralaminar, reticular, and some areas of the ventral anterior nuclei mediate general cortical alerting responses

points.text: The anterior nucleus is more consistently tied to memory and executive function loss.
points.quote: Lesions of the anterior nucleus are more consistently associated with memory and executive function loss

points.text: VPL handles spinothalamic and medial lemniscus input; head receptors reach VPM through trigeminothalamic pathways.
points.quote: The ventroposterolateral nucleus processes somatosensory information conveyed by the spinothalamic tract and medial lemniscus.

points.text: Within the ventroposterior nucleus the head is anteroinferomedial and the leg posterosuperolateral, with the arm in between.
points.quote: the head is represented anteroinferomedially, whereas the leg is represented posterosuperolaterally; the arm is represented in an intermediate position

points.text: VL and ventral anterior nuclei are the keystone of two sensorimotor loops (cerebellar and basal ganglia), which lie close together in the thalamus.
points.quote: The VL and ventral anterior regions of the thalamus constitute the keystone for two large sensorimotor control loops

points.text: The oral VL receives pallidal input and projects to premotor cortex.
points.quote: The oral portion receives input from the globus pallidus and projects mostly to the premotor cortex.

points.text: The intermediate VL (VIM) receives cerebellar input and projects to primary motor cortex.
points.quote: The intermediate portion receives input from the cerebellum and projects to the precentral, primary motor cortex (area 4)

points.text: The pulvinar is the largest thalamic nucleus and an association nucleus modulating occipito-temporo-parietal cortex.
points.quote: the largest thalamic nucleus, the pulvinar, which comprises 30% of the thalamus

localizationRules.explanation: Thalamic arteries come from the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries, and their pattern varies between people.
localizationRules.quote: The thalamic arteries arise from the posterior communicating arteries and the perimesencephalic segment of the posterior cerebral arteries

localizationRules.rule: Carotid branches rarely infarct the thalamus
localizationRules.explanation: Most thalamic supply is vertebrobasilar; the anterior choroidal artery usually supplies only part of the lateral geniculate body.
localizationRules.quote: Only the lateral portion and the hilium of the lateral geniculate body are usually fed by the anterior choroidal artery

localizationRules.rule: One posterior cerebral occlusion can be bilateral
localizationRules.explanation: Paramedian vessels often arise from a single pedicle (artery of Percheron), so a unilateral PCA occlusion can give bilateral paramedian infarcts.
localizationRules.quote: Thus, unilateral posterior cerebral artery occlusions may result in bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts

localizationRules.rule: Lateral lesions can mimic internal capsule disease
localizationRules.explanation: Laterally placed lesions may disrupt the internal capsule and produce motor and sensory deficits that mask thalamic signs.
localizationRules.quote: Laterally located lesions may disrupt the internal capsule, thereby causing motor and sensory deficits

localizationRules.explanation: Except for sensory loss, unilateral thalamic lesions give transient deficits; bilateral lesions or compression can produce coma or akinetic mutism.
localizationRules.quote: Except for sensory deficits, unilateral thalamic lesions result in transient deficits.

keySyndromes.name: Paramedian territory infarct
keySyndromes.triad: Somnolent apathy or transient coma + Memory loss + Abnormalities of vertical gaze
keySyndromes.clue: Often also involves the paramedian midbrain; causes include top-of-the-basilar embolism, atheroma at the PCA origin or artery of Percheron occlusion.
keySyndromes.quote: Most often, the syndrome is composed of the clinical triad of somnolent apathy or transient coma, memory loss, and abnormalities of vertical gaze

keySyndromes.name: Thalamogeniculate (inferolateral) territory
keySyndromes.triad: Hemianesthesia + Transient slight hemiparesis + Hemiataxia + Choreoathetoid movements + Thalamic pain with dysesthesias and allodynia
keySyndromes.clue: Components of the classic Dejerine-Roussy syndrome; all findings are contralateral to the lesioned thalamus, and lacunar forms may give pure sensory or sensorimotor stroke.
keySyndromes.quote: Ischemia in this territory (ventroposterior nucleus, VL nucleus, and subthalamic region) causes some of the components of the classic thalamic syndrome

keySyndromes.name: Tuberothalamic (anterolateral) territory
keySyndromes.triad: Apathy and verbal perseveration + Anterograde memory loss + Facial paresis for emotional movement
keySyndromes.clue: Mainly neuropsychological: language impairment with left-sided lesions, hemineglect and impaired visuospatial processing with right-sided lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: Infarcts in this territory are due to thalamopolar artery lesions and result primarily in neuropsychological dysfunction

keySyndromes.name: Lateral posterior choroidal artery territory
keySyndromes.triad: Homonymous quadrantanopsia or horizontal sectoranopia + Decreased optokinetic nystagmus when the drum moves to the side of the lesion + Hemisensory loss with mild hemiparesis + Transcortical aphasia
keySyndromes.clue: A homonymous horizontal sectoranopia is particularly suggestive of lateral geniculate body involvement.
keySyndromes.quote: Homonymous quadrantanopsia, superior or inferior, or, rarely but particularly suggestive of involvement of the lateral geniculate body in this territory, a homonymous horizontal sectoranopia

keySyndromes.name: Thalamic astasia (posterolateral thalamus)
keySyndromes.triad: Transient inability to stand or sit with normal limb strength + Falling backward or toward the contralateral side + Deficit of overlearned axial and postural movements
keySyndromes.clue: Patients are alert with normal or near-normal strength; the lesions primarily involve the superoposterolateral thalamus and spare the rubral region.
keySyndromes.quote: They fall backward or toward the side contralateral to the lesion and have a deficit of overlearned motor activity

keySyndromes.name: Thalamic aphasia (dominant thalamus)
keySyndromes.triad: Reduced spontaneous speech with paraphasic errors and perseveration + Impaired auditory comprehension + Preserved repetition and reading + Distractibility
keySyndromes.clue: Would be classified as a mixed transcortical aphasia and tends to improve in a few weeks.
keySyndromes.quote: Dominant hemisphere thalamic lesions may cause a transient language disturbance (thalamic aphasia)

boardTraps.text: Paramedian lesions often extend into the midbrain and lower alertness so much that other thalamic motor or sensory findings cannot be elicited.
boardTraps.quote: Thus, other motor or sensory findings that would point to thalamic involvement cannot be elicited.

boardTraps.text: VL lesions can look like hemiplegia because the limbs are not used in automatic movements, yet purely thalamic involvement does not cause hemiparesis; capsular extension does.
boardTraps.quote: the failure to use the limbs contralateral to the lesion may convey to the examiner the false impression that the patient is hemiplegic

boardTraps.text: Small pupils reacting well to light (diencephalic pupils) occur with reticular activating system depression or involvement of both thalami.
boardTraps.quote: Depression of the reticular activating system (most often metabolic in nature) or involvement of both thalami results in small pupils

boardTraps.text: Vertical gaze palsy with thalamic lesions usually reflects extension into the upper midbrain rather than thalamic injury itself.
boardTraps.quote: vertical gaze palsies, not due to thalamic injury per se but due to extension of the lesions into the upper midbrain

boardTraps.text: Persistent memory loss in paramedian syndromes points to the dominant anterior nucleus or mammillothalamic tract; otherwise memory loss is usually partly transient.
boardTraps.quote: Persistent memory loss is observed only with damage of the dominant anterior nucleus or mammillothalamic tract

boardTraps.text: Central poststroke pain can mimic thalamic pain: delayed pain may follow parietal cortical infarcts (pseudothalamic syndrome).
boardTraps.quote: delayed pain may follow cortical parietal infarcts, particularly those in the bank of the Sylvian fissure, affecting the second somatosensory area

19.title: Basal Ganglia
19.subtitle: Match a movement disorder (chorea, ballism, dystonia, parkinsonism) to its likely nucleus and to the syndrome that mimics it

points.text: Strict basal ganglia = caudate, putamen and globus pallidus in the cerebrum, plus the substantia nigra in the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain.
points.quote: refer to the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus (GP) in the cerebrum; the substantia nigra (SN) in the cerebral peduncles

points.text: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) belongs to the group but sits in the diencephalon.
points.quote: the substantia nigra (SN) in the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain; and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in the diencephalon

points.text: Caudate plus putamen form the striatum, which is the main input station of the basal ganglia.
points.quote: The striatum (putamen and caudate nucleus) is the main input to the basal ganglia.

points.text: Striatal subregions have different functional associations: ventral striatum with reward, caudate with cognition, putamen with motor control.
points.quote: The ventral striatum, which includes the nucleus accumbens, is associated with reward; the caudate nucleus with cognition; and the putamen with motor control

points.text: The dopaminergic nigrostriatal pathway runs from the SNpc to caudate, putamen and GP.
points.quote: The dopamine-rich nigrostriatal pathway projects from cell bodies in the SNpc to terminals in the caudate nucleus, putamen, and GP.

points.text: Main outputs leave via the GPI and SNpr to the thalamus, and from the thalamus to frontal cortical areas.
points.quote: Main outputs from the GPI and SNpr project to the thalamus and from the thalamus to various cortical areas of the frontal lobe

points.text: The principal pallidal output goes from the GPI to the VA and VL thalamic nuclei, which is why it strongly influences motor activity.
points.quote: The main output arises from the GPI to the ventral anterior (VA) and ventral lateral (VL) thalamic nuclei.

points.text: GPI efferents also reach the centrum median, which projects back to the putamen, closing a loop.
points.quote: A loop is thus formed: putamen-GPI-centrum median-putamen.

points.text: A second loop links the GPE and STN with both pallidal segments.
points.quote: Thus, another loop is formed: GPE-STN-both GP.

points.text: As worded in the book, imbalance between its two striatal pathways is linked to the clinical picture: overactive direct pathway with dystonia, overactive indirect pathway (direct hypoactive) with parkinsonism.
points.quote: when the “direct pathway” is overactive, dystonia emerges; when the “indirect pathway” is overactive (and the direct pathway is hypoactive), parkinsonism emerges

points.text: Basal ganglia pathology is often diffuse; when discrete lesions occur they commonly spill into neighboring structures, which blurs the clinical picture.
points.quote: When discrete, they often involve neighboring structures such as the internal capsule, hypothalamus, and cerebral hemispheric white matter

localizationRules.explanation: Except for hemiballism (contralateral STN or neighbors), do not expect a precise one-to-one link between the damaged nucleus and the type of movement disorder.
localizationRules.quote: Except for hemiballism, often due to damage of the contralateral STN or neighboring structures, precise topographical correlation

localizationRules.explanation: A unilateral GP lesion gives a contralateral hemi-syndrome; bilateral lesions give the bilateral akinetic or dystonic picture.
localizationRules.quote: Unilateral GP lesions cause contralateral hemidystonia, hemiparkinsonism, or tremor; bilateral lesions result in dystonia, parkinsonism, abulia, or akinesia

localizationRules.rule: Caudate behavior, putamen and GP movement
localizationRules.explanation: In the early lesion study quoted by the book, caudate damage leaned toward behavioral change and putaminal or pallidal damage toward dystonia.
localizationRules.quote: Behavioral disorders were often associated with caudate lesions, whereas dystonia and, less commonly, parkinsonism often resulted from putaminal and GP lesions

localizationRules.rule: Hemidystonia points to the contralateral striatum or thalamus
localizationRules.explanation: Contralateral hemidystonia should make you look at caudate, putamen and thalamus; stroke, trauma and perinatal injury are the most common causes listed.
localizationRules.quote: Hemidystonia may follow lesions of the contralateral caudate, putamen, or thalamus

localizationRules.rule: Extensive bilateral striatopallidal damage gives akinetic-rigid syndrome
localizationRules.explanation: Parkinsonism is not specific to Parkinson disease: widespread bilateral disruption of the striatopallidal complex or its outputs can produce it.
localizationRules.quote: any disorder leading to extensive bilateral disruption of the striatopallidal complex or its outputs may result in an akinetic-rigid syndrome

keySyndromes.name: Hemiballism (classically contralateral STN)
keySyndromes.triad: Sudden, paroxysmal, large-amplitude flinging movements of arm and leg + persists in wakefulness and ceases in sleep + often hypotonia of the involved limbs
keySyndromes.clue: Traditionally attributed to a contralateral STN lesion or its connections, but caudate, putamen, GP, precentral gyrus and thalamic lesions have also been described. Vascular STN lesions involve branches of the posterior thalamoperforators, posterior communicating or anterior choroidal arteries.
keySyndromes.quote: Hemiballism persists during wakefulness, ceases during sleep, and is often associated with hypotonia of the involved limbs.

keySyndromes.name: Huntington disease (chorea, caudate atrophy)
keySyndromes.triad: Progressive chorea + dystonia + eye movement abnormalities + mental inflexibility + irritability + personality changes + progressive dementia
keySyndromes.clue: Truncal involvement predominates in Huntington chorea, distal appendicular in Sydenham chorea. Saccades are slow and pursuit is disrupted by saccadic intrusions; juvenile onset (before age 21) shows bradykinesia, rigidity and dystonia with severe caudate atrophy.
keySyndromes.quote: typically characterized by progressive chorea, dystonia, eye movement abnormalities, mental inflexibility, irritability, personality changes, and progressive dementia

keySyndromes.name: Sydenham chorea
keySyndromes.triad: Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal link + childhood or adolescent onset + predominantly or exclusively unilateral chorea (hemichorea) + apparent flaccid paralysis (chorea mollis)
keySyndromes.clue: Hypotonia is the associated tone change, distal limbs are mainly involved, and some patients show hung-up patellar reflexes, unlike the truncal predominance of Huntington chorea.
keySyndromes.quote: Sydenham chorea is predominantly or exclusively unilateral (hemichorea) and may result in apparent flaccid paralysis (chorea mollis)

keySyndromes.name: Parkinsonism / Parkinson disease (SN dopamine loss)
keySyndromes.triad: Bradykinesia + rigidity + resting tremor + freezing + flexed posture of neck, trunk and limbs + impaired postural reflexes
keySyndromes.clue: Bradykinesia is the most disabling feature. Rest tremor is 3.5 to 7.0 Hz, often begins unilaterally in the hands and then spreads to the ipsilateral leg. PD is the prototypic akinetic-rigid syndrome from loss of dopamine-producing cells in the SN.
keySyndromes.quote: Bradykinesia; rigidity; resting tremor; freezing; flexed posture of the neck, trunk, and limbs; and impaired postural reflexes are cardinal features of parkinsonism

keySyndromes.name: Progressive supranuclear palsy (Steele-Richardson-Olszewski)
keySyndromes.triad: Symmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome + vertical supranuclear ophthalmoplegia + early falls
keySyndromes.clue: Downward saccades are affected first. Tremor is usually absent, and the gait is stiff and broad-based with extended knees and trunk, unlike the short shuffling steps and stooped posture of PD.
keySyndromes.quote: is characterized by a symmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome, vertical supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, and early falls

keySyndromes.name: Corticobasal (cortical-basal ganglionic) degeneration
keySyndromes.triad: Asymmetric parkinsonism unresponsive to levodopa + limb ideomotor apraxia + alien limb phenomenon + action-induced myoclonus + dystonia + cortical sensory loss
keySyndromes.clue: Combines cortical and basal ganglionic signs; typically starts with unilateral arm clumsiness, stiffness or jerking. Alien limb helps separate it from PSP, though arm levitation can sometimes occur in PSP.
keySyndromes.quote: The clinical hallmark of CBGD is asymmetric parkinsonism, unresponsive to levodopa

boardTraps.text: Hemiballism is not proof of an STN lesion: the book notes it often arises outside the STN, and even an ipsilateral STN infarction has been described.
boardTraps.quote: However, hemiballism often results from lesions outside the STN

boardTraps.text: Pseudoathetosis (writhing of outstretched hands) is a sensory problem, not a basal ganglia one: think proprioceptive pathway damage from nerve to parietal lobe.
boardTraps.quote: Pseudoathetosis results from faulty proprioception due to damage to large peripheral nerve fibers, dorsal root ganglia, dorsal columns/medial lemniscal pathway, or the parietal lobes

boardTraps.text: Tardive dyskinesia behaves paradoxically with the offending drug: stopping it tends to worsen the movements and increasing it tends to suppress them.
boardTraps.quote: Withdrawing the offending drug often exacerbates the severity of the involuntary movements, whereas increasing the dose lessens them.

boardTraps.text: Chorea does not map neatly onto caudate and putamen, because the diseases that cause it damage several structures at once.
boardTraps.quote: Evidence linking choreiform dyskinesias to caudate and putaminal damage is by no means convincing

boardTraps.text: Adult-onset primary dystonia usually spares the legs, so foot dystonia in an adult should prompt a search for a secondary cause.
boardTraps.quote: Foot dystonia in an adult should suggest a secondary cause

boardTraps.text: To separate PSP from PD, look for unstable gait, absence of tremor-dominant disease and lack of levodopa response.
boardTraps.quote: Unstable gait, lack of tremor-dominant disease, and no response to levodopa differentiated PSP from PD.

20.title: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
20.subtitle: Lobar landmarks, aphasias, agnosias, neglect, apraxias and frontal syndromes: what each cortical region tells you

points.text: On the lateral surface the Sylvian fissure and the Rolandic (central) sulcus separate the temporal, frontal and parietal lobes; the occipital lobe is the most posterior part.
points.quote: the frontal lobe, anterior to the Rolandic or central sulcus; and the parietal lobe, posterior to the Rolandic sulcus

points.text: The precentral gyrus holds the primary motor area.
points.quote: The precentral gyrus contains the primary motor area

points.text: Heschl transverse gyrus is the primary auditory area and forms the anterior limit of the planum temporale.
points.quote: It is the primary auditory area and the anterior limit of the planum temporale or supratemporal plane

points.text: The lowest part of the postcentral gyrus, next to the Sylvian fissure, is the secondary somatosensory cortex.
points.quote: The most inferior extent of this gyrus, abutting the Sylvian fissure, contains the secondary somatosensory cortex.

points.text: The inferior parietal lobule wraps around the end of the Sylvian sulcus anteriorly as the supramarginal gyrus (and posteriorly around the superior temporal sulcus as the angular gyrus).
points.quote: Anteriorly, the inferior parietal lobule curves around the posterior extent of the Sylvian sulcus (supramarginal gyrus)

coreAnatomy.title: Primary, secondary and multimodal association cortex

points.text: Primary areas receive sensory input or project to motor nuclei; the rest of the cortex is association cortex, which mainly makes corticocortical connections.
points.quote: contrast with the rest of the cortex, named association cortex, giving rise preferentially to corticocortical connections

points.text: Cortex next to a primary sensory area handles one modality (unimodal).
points.quote: the cortex adjacent to the primary sensory areas (secondary sensory areas) processes unimodal sensory information, often keeping a somatotopic organization

points.text: Cortex between the secondary areas is tertiary and combines modalities.
points.quote: whereas the cortex lying between the different secondary sensory areas (tertiary sensory cortex) integrates multimodal sensory information

points.text: Somatosensory information joins auditory and visual information in the angular gyrus.
points.quote: Somatotopic information is integrated with auditory and visual information in the inferoposterior portions of the inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus)

points.text: A primary lesion causes loss of the modality, whereas a multimodal association lesion produces deficits of integrated performance.
points.quote: Lesions of the primary somatosensory area result in sensory loss, whereas lesions in the multimodal association areas result in motor performances

points.text: The right hemisphere is dominant for spatial and constructional skills, directed attention and body image.
points.quote: the right hemisphere is dominant for tasks requiring spatial and constructional skills, as well as for directed attention and body image

points.text: The left hemisphere is dominant for language, motor functions and linguistic reasoning.
points.quote: whereas the left hemisphere is dominant for language and motor functions, as well as linguistic thought and reasoning

points.text: Wernicke area (area 22) is the posterior superior temporal auditory association cortex; its infarction gives the greatest impairment of auditory comprehension.
points.quote: Ischemia or infarction centered in the posterior two-thirds of the superior temporal gyrus affecting the auditory association cortex

points.text: Broca area is the inferior left frontal gyrus (areas 44 and 45); true Broca aphasia needs more extensive damage around it.
points.quote: extensive damage involving not only Broca area (the inferior left frontal gyrus, which contains areas 44 and 45)

points.text: Active, goal-directed attention uses a dorsal system and involves both hemispheres.
points.quote: Active attention is mediated by a dorsal system including the superior parietal lobule and the superior portion of the dorsal prefrontal cortex

points.text: Because the right hemisphere alerts for both sides of the body, attentional impairment is more frequent and more pervasive with right-sided lesions.
points.quote: As the right hemisphere provides alerting mechanisms for both sides of the body, attentional impairment occurs more often and is more pervasive

points.text: A unilateral mesencephalic reticular lesion can produce contralateral inattention through hypoarousal of the hemisphere.
points.quote: unilateral lesions of the mesencephalic reticular formation result in contralateral inattention, probably because of unilateral hypoarousal of the hemisphere

coreAnatomy.title: Frontal motor organization and memory circuits

points.text: Large bilateral mesial frontal (cingulate, supplementary motor) lesions leave an alert-looking patient motionless and mute.
points.quote: Although seemingly alert, patients with large bilateral lesions in this region remain motionless and mute (akinetic mutism)

points.text: The primary motor cortex is more important for fine distal movements; axial movements such as walking depend more on subcortical structures.
points.quote: The primary motor cortex plays a greater role in the execution of fine, distal movements

points.text: The amnestic syndrome arises from damage to medial temporal structures, anteromedial thalamic nuclei or their connections.
points.quote: damage the medial temporal lobes, especially the amygdala and hippocampus; the anterior and dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus; or the connections of these structures

points.text: Bilateral lesions of Papez circuit structures have been reported to cause amnesia.
points.quote: lesions, usually bilateral, of any of the structures of Papez circuit (hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract,

localizationRules.explanation: Seizures plus multimodal deficits (aphasia, apraxia) point to cortex; weakness, spasticity, field deficits, pure motor syndromes and urinary incontinence point to white matter.
localizationRules.quote: Characteristic of cortical lesions are (1) seizures and (2) multimodal motor and sensory deficits, such as aphasia and apraxia.

localizationRules.rule: Tempo and nature of the lesion
localizationRules.explanation: A sudden destructive lesion gives a more severe deficit than a slowly infiltrating tumor in the same place, so localization of diffuse lesions is less accurate.
localizationRules.quote: small infarcts often cause aphasia, but tumors have to be quite large before they cause an aphasic syndrome

localizationRules.rule: Do not pinpoint a square centimeter
localizationRules.explanation: Cortical functions are subserved by networks and vary between individuals, so name the likely region, not the exact spot.
localizationRules.quote: any attempt to pinpoint the exact square centimeter of the cortex that accounts for a deficit in a particular patient is a futile endeavor

localizationRules.rule: Temporal lesion gives sensory aphasia, frontal gives motor aphasia
localizationRules.explanation: Posterior (temporal) lesions impair comprehension of the spoken word; frontal lesions give sparse agrammatical language with comprehension spared.
localizationRules.quote: patients with predominantly temporal lesions had a sensory or receptive aphasia, interfering with the comprehension of the spoken word

localizationRules.explanation: Global aphasia with hemiplegia means damage to the anterior language area, the basal ganglia region, the insula and the posterior language region, usually a large MCA infarct.
localizationRules.quote: The presence or absence of hemiplegia is an important clue to the localization of brain damage

localizationRules.rule: Neglect points to the right inferior parietal lobule
localizationRules.explanation: Neglect appears more readily and profoundly with right-hemisphere lesions; the right inferior parietal lobule is the classic site.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of the right inferior parietal lobule are especially apt to cause this syndrome.

localizationRules.rule: Primary cortex versus unimodal association cortex
localizationRules.explanation: A primary lesion causes loss of that modality; an association-cortex lesion causes extinction on double simultaneous stimulation (visual areas 18 and 19; anterior parietal for touch).
localizationRules.quote: Whereas unilateral lesions of primary cortex cause contralateral unimodal sensory loss, lesions of unimodal association cortex impair the perception of contralateral versus ipsilateral stimuli

keySyndromes.name: Wernicke aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Fluent speech + impaired repetition + impaired naming + paraphasic errors (impaired comprehension)
keySyndromes.clue: Posterior superior temporal lesion, most commonly from an inferior division MCA infarct; hemiparesis and sensory loss may be absent or mild, so it can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with Wernicke aphasia are unable to repeat sentences correctly, to assemble phonemes correctly, and to name things properly, but their speech is fluent

keySyndromes.name: Broca aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Drastic loss of fluency + agrammatic telegraphic speech + impaired repetition + impaired naming helped by cueing
keySyndromes.clue: Lasting Broca aphasia corresponds to lesions extending across the frontoparietal operculum, not to Broca area alone.
keySyndromes.quote: There is a drastic loss of speech fluency, with speech becoming effortful and often slow, with pauses between words often outnumbering the words themselves

keySyndromes.name: Conduction aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Intelligible speech + good enough comprehension + impaired repetition + paraphasic errors
keySyndromes.clue: Circumscribed lesions of the supramarginal gyrus (area 40) or auditory cortex; the book notes the traditional arcuate fasciculus explanation is not well supported.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with conduction aphasia speak intelligibly and comprehend well enough to maintain a normal conversation, but their ability to repeat is impaired

keySyndromes.name: Transcortical sensory aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Good repetition + impaired comprehension of spoken and written words + echolalia
keySyndromes.clue: Analogue of Wernicke aphasia with spared repetition; posterior left middle temporal and angular gyrus region, with little localizing value, often MCA/PCA watershed ischemia.
keySyndromes.quote: Some patients can repeat words well but are unable to understand the meaning of the spoken or written word

keySyndromes.name: Transcortical motor aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Lack of verbal spontaneity + correct repetition + telegraphic speech or perseveration
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant frontal lesion anterior or superior to Broca area, or supplementary motor area; ACA infarct or ACA-MCA border zone.
keySyndromes.quote: transcortical motor aphasia differs from Broca in that the patient can repeat correctly and may even correct syntactic errors in the original sentence

keySyndromes.name: Alexia without agraphia (pure word blindness)
keySyndromes.triad: Cannot read + writes on dictation + usually right homonymous hemianopia or hemiachromatopsia + often color agnosia
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant medial occipital lesion plus the inferior splenium disconnects visual input from the intact dominant angular gyrus; alexia with agraphia is the angular gyrus syndrome instead.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients cannot read but are able to write on dictation.

keySyndromes.name: Balint syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Failure to shift gaze (apraxia of gaze) + optic ataxia + decreased visual attention with tunnel vision
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral parietooccipital convexity lesions (watershed) and often visual simultanagnosia.
keySyndromes.quote: the Balint syndrome, which follows bilateral parietooccipital lesions in the convexity of the hemispheres

keySyndromes.name: Gerstmann syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Finger agnosia + right-left disorientation + agraphia + acalculia
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant angular and supramarginal gyri; the book cites necropsy cases with all four signs and an intact angular gyrus.
keySyndromes.quote: Gerstmann described the association of these four signs (Gerstmann syndrome) as characteristic of lesions in the angular and supramarginal gyri

boardTraps.text: A lesion restricted to Broca area or its subjacent white matter does not produce true, lasting Broca aphasia, only a mild transient aphasia.
boardTraps.quote: When damage is restricted to Brocas area alone or to its subjacent white matter, true Broca aphasia does not develop

boardTraps.text: Acute global aphasia after a large perisylvian stroke often evolves into Broca aphasia as comprehension improves, so the label depends on timing.
boardTraps.quote: Acutely after stroke, patients that will eventually develop classical Broca aphasia often have global aphasia.

boardTraps.text: Global aphasia without hemiparesis is possible: it may be a single dominant temporoparietal lesion, but more often two discrete dominant-hemisphere lesions, one frontal and one temporoparietal (usually embolic).
boardTraps.quote: Global aphasia without other lateralizing signs (i.e., no hemiparesis or lasting motor defects) may occur with a single dominant temporoparietal lesion

boardTraps.text: Visual inattention can masquerade as hemianopia; a patient may detect a left-field stimulus when the eyes are turned to the right, so the hemispace of presentation matters.
boardTraps.quote: This patient had hemispatial visual inattention masquerading as hemianopia.

boardTraps.text: Anosognosia is often seen with right-hemisphere lesions but does not require neglect.
boardTraps.quote: However, it need not be associated with a neglect syndrome, and often it is not

boardTraps.text: Anton syndrome: a patient who is blind from bilateral extensive medial occipital lesions denies the blindness and confabulates; discrete lesions usually extend to areas 18 and 19.
boardTraps.quote: Patients with acute, bilateral, and extensive medial occipital lesions that render them blind may deny having any difficulty with seeing (visual anosognosia) and confabulate

boardTraps.text: Subcortical aphasia is debated: the book calls it controversial whether pure subcortical lesions can cause true aphasia, and notes that MCA stem occlusion also ischemias the posterior perisylvian cortex.
boardTraps.quote: It is controversial whether pure subcortical lesions can cause true aphasia

21.title: Localization of Lesions in the Autonomic Nervous System
21.subtitle: A stepwise approach to locating autonomic dysfunction from cortex and hypothalamus to ganglia, nerves and gut

points.text: The ANS has sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric divisions.
points.quote: The ANS consists of three anatomically distinct divisions: the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS), and the enteric nervous system (ENS).

points.text: Sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways use a two-neuron chain (preganglionic then postganglionic) between the CNS and the effector.
points.quote: The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions have two-neuron series between the central nervous system (CNS) and the effector organs.

points.text: A central autonomic network is bidirectionally connected with the ANS and includes cortical, amygdala, hypothalamic and brainstem nodes.
points.quote: The ANS is bidirectionally connected with a central autonomic network that includes the medial prefrontal and insular cortices, the central nucleus of the amygdala

points.text: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies lie in the intermediolateral column of the cord (T1-L2).
points.quote: Most sympathetic preganglionic neurons (primary efferent neurons) have their cell bodies in the intermediolateral gray cell column

points.text: Rostral sympathetic neurons serve head and neck, caudal ones serve thoracic, abdominal and pelvic viscera.
points.quote: Rostrally placed neurons innervate head and neck structures, whereas neurons caudally located innervate the heart, lungs, and abdominal and pelvic viscera.

points.text: Some postganglionic sympathetic fibers are cholinergic: those to sweat glands, piloerector muscles and a few blood vessels.
points.quote: Postganglionic sympathetic nerve fibers to sweat glands, piloerector muscles, and a few blood vessels are cholinergic.

points.text: Cranial parasympathetic outflow runs in CN III, VII, IX and X, and the vagus carries most parasympathetic fibers.
points.quote: Most parasympathetic fibers are carried by the vagus nerve (CN X).

points.text: Sacral parasympathetic neurons lie at S2-S4 and supply pelvic organs through the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
points.quote: The sacral parasympathetic division is localized in the sacral intermediolateral cell columns of the second to fourth segments (S2-S4) of the spinal cord.

points.text: Insular strokes have been linked to cardiovascular complications.
points.quote: Insular cortex strokes have been associated with arterial hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, increased risk of myocardial injury

points.text: The hypothalamus is the highest integration level; its paraventricular nucleus is a key center for cardiovascular regulation.
points.quote: the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus has emerged as one of the most important centers involved in cardiovascular regulation

points.text: In the periaqueductal gray, dorsolateral and ventrolateral zones have opposite cardiovascular effects on chemical stimulation.
points.quote: Chemical stimulation of the dorsolateral gray results in hypertension and tachycardia, whereas activation of the ventrolateral gray results in the opposite effects.

points.text: The nucleus tractus solitarius is a sensory nucleus whose bilateral lesions may cause acute neurogenic hypertension.
points.quote: Bilateral lesions of the nucleus tractus solitarius may result in acute neurogenic hypertension

localizationRules.rule: Ask where in the pathway the lesion sits
localizationRules.explanation: After deciding which division (SNS, PNS, ENS) is involved and whether it is failure or hyperactivity, place the lesion along the pathway.
localizationRules.quote: Is the ANS involvement central, preganglionic, ganglionic, postganglionic, or localized to the neuroeffectors?

localizationRules.explanation: Describe it as focal or generalized, its time course, and primary or secondary, then look for underactivity or failure.
localizationRules.quote: Autonomic dysfunction may be focal or generalized; acute, subacute, or chronic; primary or secondary

localizationRules.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall in blood pressure within 3 minutes of standing, and it often has several causes.
localizationRules.quote: defined as a sustained drop in the systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥20 mm Hg or the diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of ≥10 mm Hg

localizationRules.rule: Hypothalamic descending sympathetic fibers are uncrossed
localizationRules.explanation: They descend through the lateral brainstem tegmentum and lateral medulla to the autonomic outflows, so lateral brainstem lesions may interrupt them.
localizationRules.quote: Descending hypothalamic sympathetic fibers are uncrossed and, by way of the lateral brainstem tegmentum and lateral medullary formation

keySyndromes.name: Gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome)
keySyndromes.triad: Rare complication of surgery in or near the parotid gland + Sweating and flushing of the temporal and retroauricular area + Triggered by sour, spicy or salty foods
keySyndromes.clue: Thought to result from simultaneous damage to sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves near the parotid gland.
keySyndromes.quote: Gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome) is a rare complication of surgery in or near the parotid gland

keySyndromes.name: Crocodile tears (Bogorad syndrome)
keySyndromes.triad: Complication of recovering Bell palsy + Profuse lacrimation during eating or drinking
keySyndromes.clue: Caused by misdirected regeneration of autonomic fibers to the lacrimal rather than the submandibular gland.
keySyndromes.quote: It is caused by a misdirection of regenerating autonomic fibers to the lacrimal gland instead of the submandibular gland

keySyndromes.name: Insular cortex stroke
keySyndromes.triad: Arterial hypertension + Cardiac arrhythmias + Increased risk of myocardial injury + Raised catecholamines + Susceptibility to sudden death
keySyndromes.clue: The insula is described as the most important cortical area for cardiovascular regulation.
keySyndromes.quote: increased risk of myocardial injury, raised catecholamines levels, and increased susceptibility to sudden death

keySyndromes.name: Dopamine beta hydroxylase (DBH) deficiency
keySyndromes.triad: Autonomic failure + Normal parasympathetic function + Normal sympathetic cholinergic function + Absent sympathetic noradrenergic function
keySyndromes.clue: Autosomal recessive; listed among neurologic causes of orthostatic hypotension.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with autonomic failure due to DBH have normal parasympathetic and sympathetic cholinergic function but lack sympathetic noradrenergic function

keySyndromes.name: Acute porphyric neuropathy
keySyndromes.triad: Abdominal pain (the commonest) + Severe vomiting + Constipation and occasional diarrhea + Inappropriate sinus tachycardia + Labile hypertension + Bladder dysfunction
keySyndromes.clue: Autonomic dysfunction is mainly due to vagal insufficiency.
keySyndromes.quote: In acute porphyric neuropathy, the autonomic dysfunction is mainly the result of vagal insufficiency

keySyndromes.name: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy
keySyndromes.triad: Autonomic failure + High titers of ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibody
keySyndromes.clue: A severe but potentially treatable antibody-mediated cause of autonomic failure (ganglionic level).
keySyndromes.quote: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathies, associated with high titers of ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibody (g-AChR antibody), represent examples of severe but potentially treatable

boardTraps.text: Not every orthostatic hypotension is neurogenic: drugs, hypovolemia, impaired venous return and cardiac pump failure must be considered.
boardTraps.quote: Several causes of orthostatic hypotension or worsening hypotension are nonneurogenic and include drugs (vasodilators, diuretics, dopaminergic agents, sildenafil, chemotherapeutic agents), hypovolemia

boardTraps.text: Orthostatic hypotension can coexist with supine hypertension.
boardTraps.quote: Not uncommonly, orthostatic hypotension occurs concomitantly with supine hypertension

boardTraps.text: Within the medulla, the rostral level of nucleus ambiguus involvement is more likely to cause dysphagia than the middle-lower segment.
boardTraps.quote: Involvement of the nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla oblongata is more likely to result in dysphagia

boardTraps.text: Autonomic neuropathies usually accompany a somatic neuropathy, but they may be isolated.
boardTraps.quote: Most autonomic neuropathies occur in association with a somatic neuropathy, but they may present in isolation.

boardTraps.text: Primary hyperhidrosis mainly involves the axillae, palms and soles and is characterized by excessive, uncontrolled sweat production.
boardTraps.quote: Primary hyperhidrosis, a common and troublesome condition, primarily involves the axillae as well as the palms and soles

boardTraps.text: In small-fiber neuropathies, sudomotor dysfunction is among the earliest neurophysiologic abnormalities.
boardTraps.quote: sudomotor dysfunction is one of the earliest neurophysiologic abnormalities in these neuropathies

22.title: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and Cerebellum
22.subtitle: Match the deficit pattern to the arterial territory: ICA, AChA, ACA, MCA, PCA, thalamic, vertebrobasilar, border zone and lacunar syndromes

points.text: The ACA supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere and the upper frontal and parietal regions.
points.quote: The ACAs supply the medial surface of the cerebrum and the upper regions of the frontal and parietal lobes

points.text: The MCA covers most of the lateral hemispheric surface plus deep frontal and parietal structures.
points.quote: The MCA supplies most of the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere and deep frontal and parietal lobe structures

points.text: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe, the inferior and medial temporal lobe, and parts of the midbrain and thalamus.
points.quote: The PCAs supply the occipital lobes, inferior and medial surface of the temporal lobes, parts of the midbrain and thalamus

points.text: The striatum and thalamus get three groups of perforators: ACA (medial striate), MCA stem (lateral striate) and PCA (posterior striate).
points.quote: medial striate arteries from the proximal ACA; lateral striate arteries from the MCA stem; and posterior striate arteries from the PCAs

points.text: Perforators from the M1 segment of the MCA feed the corona radiata, external capsule, claustrum, putamen, part of the pallidum and the caudate body.
points.quote: Penetrating lenticulostriate arteries supplying the adjacent corona radiata, external capsule, claustrum, putamen, part of the globus pallidus, body of the caudate nucleus

points.text: The AChA feeds the visual pathway at the lateral geniculate/optic tract level and part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which explains its triad of hemiparesis, sensory loss and field defect.
points.quote: lateral geniculate body, optic tract, origin of the optic radiations, genu and inferior and medial segments of the posterior limb of the internal capsule

points.text: PICA supplies the inferior vermis and the inferior and posterior cerebellar hemispheres.
points.quote: The PICAs supply the inferior vermis and the inferior and posterior aspects of the cerebellar hemispheres

points.text: AICA supplies the ventral cerebellum, the middle cerebellar peduncle and the caudal pontine tegmentum.
points.quote: The AICAs supply the anterior surface of the simple, superior, and inferior semilunar lobules, flocculus, middle cerebellar peduncle, and caudal pontine tegmentum

points.text: SCA supplies the upper half of the cerebellum, the dentate nuclei and the rostral pontine tegmentum.
points.quote: The SCAs supply the superior half of the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, dentate nuclei, and rostral pontine tegmentum

points.text: The medulla is fed by the paired vertebral arteries and the unpaired anterior spinal artery.
points.quote: The blood supply to the medulla oblongata arises from the paired VAs and the unpaired anterior spinal artery

points.text: Brainstem blood supply is conceptually divided into four territories.
points.quote: The blood supply to the brainstem is often divided into four distinct territories: anteromedial, anterolateral, lateral, and posterior

points.text: Thalamic infarcts fall into four vascular territories, each with its own syndrome.
points.quote: Thalamic infarctions characteristically involve one of four vascular territories (Fig. 22-4): posterolateral, anterior, paramedian, or dorsal

localizationRules.rule: Amaurosis fugax points to the ICA, not the MCA
localizationRules.explanation: Transient painless monocular visual loss separates an ICA syndrome from an MCA syndrome.
localizationRules.quote: is the hallmark clinical feature that helps distinguish the ICA syndrome from the MCA syndrome

localizationRules.explanation: Both give large hemispheric strokes; reduced alertness and marked leg weakness favor a carotid terminus occlusion.
localizationRules.quote: Decreased level of alertness and severe leg weakness are useful clinical clues to differentiate a carotid T occlusion from a stem of the MCA stroke

localizationRules.rule: Faciolingual hemiparesis localizes to the capsular genu
localizationRules.explanation: Face and tongue weakness, with or without masseter, palatal, pharyngeal, laryngeal or hand weakness, suggests a genu of the internal capsule stroke.
localizationRules.quote: Faciolingual hemiparesis, whether associated with masseter, palatal, pharyngeal, laryngeal, or hand weakness, is highly suggestive of a genu of the internal capsule stroke

localizationRules.rule: Pure sensory stroke: thalamus or pons?
localizationRules.explanation: If both spinothalamic and medial lemniscal modalities are lost, think thalamus, internal capsule or corona radiata; a dissociated loss favors the brainstem (in the pontine form the book describes vibration and position sense impaired with pinprick and temperature preserved).
localizationRules.quote: Conversely, in cases of PSS involving the thalamus, internal capsule, or corona radiata, both spinothalamic and medial lemniscal modalities are compromised

localizationRules.explanation: Leg-predominant weakness with the face spared after hypotension suggests an anterior watershed lesion in the unilateral series the book reviews.
localizationRules.quote: caused crural predominant hemiparesis with facial sparing, at times associated with impaired sensation

keySyndromes.name: Anterior choroidal artery (AChA) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Hemiparesis + Hemianesthesia + Homonymous hemianopia
keySyndromes.clue: The hemianopia may spare the horizontal meridian or appear as quadruple sectoranopias, from optic tract, lateral geniculate or optic radiation involvement; the hemiparesis comes from the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
keySyndromes.quote: infarctions in the AChA territory result in hemiparesis, hemianesthesia, and homonymous hemianopia

keySyndromes.name: ACA syndrome (hemispheric branches)
keySyndromes.triad: Contralateral weakness mainly involving the leg + Abulia + Paratonia (gegenhalten) and grasp reflex
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral mesiofrontal damage adds frontal release signs, akinetic mutism, paraparesis, urinary incontinence and amnesia with apathy; Heubner-artery infarcts instead give face and arm weakness without sensory loss.
keySyndromes.quote: Involvement of hemispheric ACA branches often results in contralateral weakness mainly involving the leg

keySyndromes.name: MCA superior division syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Contralateral hemiparesis predominantly of upper extremity and face + Hemisensory loss + Conjugate gaze deviation
keySyndromes.clue: Visual fields tend to be preserved; the dominant side gives nonfluent aphasia. Inferior division strokes instead give Wernicke aphasia (left) and hemianopia or quadrantanopia.
keySyndromes.quote: results in contralateral hemiparesis with predominant involvement of the upper extremity and face, hemisensory loss, and conjugate gaze deviation

keySyndromes.name: PCA syndrome (branch occlusion)
keySyndromes.triad: Homonymous hemianopia (striate cortex, optic radiations or lateral geniculate body)
keySyndromes.clue: Macular sparing can be partial or complete if the occipital pole is spared; the defect may be limited to a homonymous quadrantanopia.
keySyndromes.quote: PCA branch occlusion may result in homonymous hemianopia due to infarction of the striate cortex, optic radiations, or lateral geniculate body

keySyndromes.name: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia + Ipsilateral lateropulsion + Ipsilateral facial hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia + Pharyngeal and palatal weakness, dysphagia, dysphonia + Ipsilateral Horner syndrome + Contralateral trunk and extremity hypalgesia and thermoanesthesia
keySyndromes.clue: No limb weakness. Opalski syndrome is the variant with ipsilateral hemiplegia from submedullary extension.
keySyndromes.quote: Wallenberg syndrome results in a constellation of signs and symptoms, including ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia, homolateral lateropulsion

keySyndromes.name: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron weakness of half of the tongue + Contralateral hemiparesis + Loss of position sense and vibration
keySyndromes.clue: The face is often spared, and the ipsilateral tongue paresis is seen in only half of the cases.
keySyndromes.quote: ipsilateral lower motor neuron weakness of half of the tongue and contralateral hemiparesis with associated loss of position sense and vibration

boardTraps.text: Bilateral ACA-MCA border zone ischemia produces bibrachial sensorimotor impairment that the book describes as often confined to the forearms and hands, together with impaired volitional saccades.
boardTraps.quote: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the ACAs and MCAs results in bibrachial cortical sensorimotor impairment often confined to the forearms and hands

boardTraps.text: Leg-predominant weakness is not specific for the ACA: only a minority of such strokes are ACA territory, and the internal capsule, corona radiata or brainstem can be responsible.
boardTraps.quote: ACA territory infarctions account for only one-fourth of all strokes associated with a pattern of leg-predominant weakness

boardTraps.text: Do not rely on a cervical bruit: its absence does not exclude carotid disease because the bruit may vanish with very tight stenosis.
boardTraps.quote: the lack of a cervical bruit has little diagnostic value because the bruit may disappear when the carotid artery stenosis is >90%

boardTraps.text: Babinski-Nageotte is not a synonym for the hemimedullary syndrome; the book defines it as Wallenberg syndrome plus a contralateral hemiplegia.
boardTraps.quote: The eponym Babinski-Nageotte syndrome has been mistakenly used as a synonymous for hemimedullary syndrome

boardTraps.text: A lacunar sensorimotor stroke involves face, arm and leg; selective face and arm involvement with the leg spared points away from a lacune.
boardTraps.quote: Selective involvement of the face and arm, sparing the leg, suggests a non-lacunar mechanism

boardTraps.text: A single transient brainstem symptom is not enough to call a vertebrobasilar TIA.
boardTraps.quote: Transient vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, or dysphagia by itself is insufficient to establish a diagnosis of vertebrobasilar artery territory transient ischemic attacks

23.title: The Localization of Lesions Causing Coma
23.subtitle: Use respiration, pupils, eye movements and limb posture to place the level of dysfunction in a patient with depressed alertness

points.text: In humans the ARAS sits in the paramedian tegmentum of the posterior pons and midbrain.
points.quote: In humans, the ARAS lies in the paramedian tegmental region of the posterior portion of pons and midbrain

points.text: The ARAS runs from the upper pons through the midbrain to the posterior hypothalamus and thalamic reticular formation.
points.quote: extends from the superior half of the pons through the midbrain to the posterior portion of the hypothalamus and to the thalamic reticular formation

points.text: Because the MLF and the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei lie among the ARAS neurons, a brainstem cause of unresponsiveness also disturbs eye movements, and the pattern of ocular motility helps place the lesion.
points.quote: Thus, when unresponsiveness is caused by brainstem damage, the lesion affects the mechanisms of ocular motility as well

points.text: Bilateral hemispheric lesions can cause transient coma, especially with mesial frontal involvement.
points.quote: Bilateral cerebral hemispheric lesions may cause transient coma, particularly when they involve the mesial frontal region

points.text: Bilateral lesions of the anterior cingulate regions, the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the pallidum or the hypothalamus cause akinetic mutism.
points.quote: Lesions that cause akinetic mutism bilaterally affect the frontal region (anterior cingulate gyri), the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the globus pallidus, or the hypothalamus

points.text: Locked-in syndrome interrupts the descending motor pathways in the basis pontis on both sides while the dorsal reticular formation is spared, so alertness is preserved.
points.quote: These lesions involve the descending motor pathways bilaterally in the basis pontis but spare the more dorsal reticular formation

points.text: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is most often linked to bilateral thalamic dysfunction and to lesions of descending pathways from the hemispheres down to the upper pons.
points.quote: bilateral thalamic dysfunction and has also been described with lesions of the descending pathways anywhere from the cerebral hemispheres to the level of the upper pons

points.text: Apneustic breathing localizes to the lateral tegmentum of the lower pons.
points.quote: This abnormality appears with lesions of the lateral tegmentum of the lower half of the pons

points.text: Cluster breathing points to the low pons or high medulla.
points.quote: Breathing with a cluster of breaths following each other in an irregular sequence may result from low pontine or high medullary lesions

points.text: Ataxic breathing signals impending respiratory failure from dorsomedial medullary damage.
points.quote: heralds complete respiratory failure and follows damage of the dorsomedial medulla

localizationRules.rule: Pontine gaze palsy cannot be overcome
localizationRules.explanation: A lower pontine tegmental lesion makes the eyes look toward the hemiparetic side; unlike hemispheric deviation, oculocephalic or caloric stimulation does not move the eyes across.
localizationRules.quote: cause a horizontal gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion so that the eyes look toward the hemiparetic side

localizationRules.rule: Isolated failure of adduction means MLF
localizationRules.explanation: With normal pupils and normal vertical movements, think MLF in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that does not adduct.
localizationRules.quote: indicates a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that fails to adduct

localizationRules.rule: An abnormal light reflex is structural until proven otherwise
localizationRules.explanation: The pupillary light reflex survives metabolic dysfunction, so an abnormal reflex, especially a unilateral one, points to the midbrain or the oculomotor nerve (with the drug exceptions the book lists).
localizationRules.quote: Abnormalities of this reflex, particularly when unilateral, indicate structural lesions of the midbrain or oculomotor nerve

localizationRules.explanation: Diencephalic dysfunction gives small reactive pupils, midbrain tegmental lesions give midsized fixed pupils, and pontine tegmental lesions give small pupils from interrupted sympathetic pathways.
localizationRules.quote: Pontine tegmental lesions cause small pupils due to interruption of descending sympathetic pathways

localizationRules.rule: Asymmetry argues against a metabolic cause
localizationRules.explanation: Focal motor asymmetry in a comatose patient suggests a structural lesion rather than metabolic encephalopathy.
localizationRules.quote: Asymmetric motor findings speak against the diagnosis of metabolic encephalopathy

keySyndromes.name: Akinetic mutism
keySyndromes.triad: Seemingly awake, silent and motionless + Eyes dart toward moving objects + Frontal release signs such as grasp or sucking reflex
keySyndromes.clue: Few signs of damaged descending motor pathways; frontal release or corticospinal signs favor akinetic mutism over catatonia, and the EEG may show slow waves whereas it is normal in catatonia.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a state in which the patient, although seemingly awake, remains silent and motionless

keySyndromes.name: Locked-in syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Mute and motionless + Awake, alert and aware of self + Impaired horizontal eye movements with vertical eye and eyelid movements preserved
keySyndromes.clue: Usually basilar artery thrombosis with ventral pontine infarction; with mesencephalic lesions there are bilateral ptosis and vertical as well as horizontal ophthalmoplegia.
keySyndromes.quote: is mute and motionless (deefferented) but remains awake, alert, aware of self, and capable of perceiving sensory stimuli

keySyndromes.name: Lateral (uncal) transtentorial herniation
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral pupil dilated and sluggish + Posterior cerebral artery occlusion with hemorrhagic mesial occipital infarct + Kernohan notch hemiparesis ipsilateral to the original lesion
keySyndromes.clue: The pupil is affected first because the third nerve is compressed; later Duret hemorrhages of the midbrain tegmentum make recovery almost impossible.
keySyndromes.quote: the ipsilateral pupil becomes progressively dilated and responds sluggishly to light

keySyndromes.name: Central transtentorial herniation
keySyndromes.triad: Early diencephalic: somnolence with tiny reactive pupils + Late diencephalic: Cheyne-Stokes breathing and decorticate posturing + Midbrain-upper pons: midsized unequal pupils and decerebrate posturing + Lower pons: no eye movements + Medullary: ataxic breathing then apnea
keySyndromes.clue: All structures at one brainstem level tend to fail together, unlike compressive posterior fossa lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: the clinical picture reflects an orderly rostrocaudal progression of brainstem

keySyndromes.name: Ocular bobbing
keySyndromes.triad: Brisk bilateral downward eye movement + Slow return to midposition
keySyndromes.clue: Typical bobbing with preserved horizontal eye movements is specific but not pathognomonic of acute pontine injury; pretectal pseudobobbing has a V pattern and pretectal signs (acute hydrocephalus).
keySyndromes.quote: Ocular bobbing refers to intermittent, often conjugate, brisk, bilateral downward movement of the eyes with slow return to midposition

keySyndromes.name: Posterior fossa compression (cerebellar hemorrhage)
keySyndromes.triad: Occipital headache + Vomiting + Ataxia
keySyndromes.clue: Unless massive, these lesions affect one brainstem level more than others, often asymmetrically, giving mainly unilateral brainstem and cerebellar signs.
keySyndromes.quote: Early in the clinical course, occipital headache, vomiting, and ataxia are usually prominent

boardTraps.text: Decorticate and decerebrate posturing are often produced by metabolic disorders, so they do not carry the structural implications suggested by their names.
boardTraps.quote: do not have the structural implications that their names, coined during experimental work, would suggest

boardTraps.text: Kernohan notch makes the hemiparesis ipsilateral to the mass; with a dilated pupil and ipsilateral hemiparesis, the lesion is on the side of the abnormal pupil.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, when a dilated pupil and hemiparesis appear ipsilaterally, the original lesion is likely to be on the side of the abnormal pupil

boardTraps.text: Wrong-way eyes: thalamic (rarely basal ganglionic) lesions, almost always hemorrhagic, can drive the eyes away from the lesion, contrary to the usual rule that the eyes look toward a hemispheric lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Thalamic and, rarely, basal ganglionic lesions, almost always hemorrhagic, may produce forced deviation of the eyes to the side contralateral to the lesion

boardTraps.text: Metabolic disease can mimic the respiratory patterns of structural lesions, so check metabolic status before localizing by breathing pattern.
boardTraps.quote: caution and a thorough evaluation of the metabolic status of the patient must guide the interpretation of respiratory changes

boardTraps.text: Raised intracranial pressure from a supratentorial lesion can falsely suggest a posterior fossa lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Sixth nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs

boardTraps.text: Fixed pupils do not by themselves prove irreversible coma in acute neurosurgical lesions.
boardTraps.quote: With acute neurosurgical lesions, fixed pupils are not necessarily a sign of irreversible coma
